bio.en: Deb Liu was VP of Product at Facebook (creating and leading Facebook Marketplace, used by 1B+ monthly), led its first mobile ad product, and is CEO of Ancestry, with board roles including Intuit.
bio.zh: Deb Liu 曾任 Facebook 产品副总裁（创建并领导月活超 10 亿的 Facebook Marketplace，并主导首个移动广告产品），现任 Ancestry CEO，并在 Intuit 等公司任董事。

summary.en: Deb shares tactical career advice, including why resilience is key and how to “PM your career like you PM your product.” She discusses succeeding in business as an introvert by reframing self-promotion as “educating others about your team's great work,” and what she learned building multiple zero-to-one billion-dollar businesses inside Facebook. The conversation is full of hard-won wisdom on career, leadership, and impact.
summary.zh: Deb 分享了务实的职业建议，包括为何韧性关键，以及如何“像做产品一样做自己的职业生涯管理”。她讨论了内向者如何在职场成功——把自我推销重新定义为“让他人了解团队的出色工作”，以及在 Facebook 内部打造多个从 0 到 1 的十亿美元业务的所学。对话充满关于职业、领导与影响力的宝贵智慧。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You're VP of product at Facebook. You're director at eBay and PayPal. You're on the board of Intuit. You've been the CEO of Ancestry now for the past three and a half years. This is a career path that a lot of people dream of.
turns.zh: 您是 Facebook 的产品副总裁。您是 eBay 和 PayPal 的总监。您是 Intuit 董事会成员。过去三年半以来，您一直担任 Ancestry 的首席执行官。这是很多人梦想的职业道路。

turns.speaker: Deb Liu
turns.en: Some of the best PMs I have ever worked with are terrible PMs for their career. They just drift from job to job. "Hey, should I take this role or this role? How do I think about this?" But if I said you had to write a spec for your career, what does success look like? How are you going to get there?
turns.zh: 我曾经共事过的一些最优秀的产品经理在他们的职业生涯中却是糟糕的产品经理。他们只是从一个工作转移到另一个工作。 “哎，我该接这个角色还是这个角色？我怎么想这个？”但如果我说你必须为你的职业生涯写一份规范，那么成功是什么样子的呢？你要怎么去那里？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You wrote this awesome post about introverts and how hard it is to be successful as an introvert.
turns.zh: 你写了这篇关于内向者以及作为一个内向者取得成功是多么困难的精彩文章。

turns.speaker: Deb Liu
turns.en: The workplace is really favoring people who can speak up. It looks like self-promotion. I wouldn't want to do that because it's self-promotion. But instead, what if I called it educating about all the great work your team has been doing? Helping people see why your team should get more resources, you have to actually share what you do.
turns.zh: 职场真的很青睐敢于发声的人。看起来像是自我推销。我不想这样做，因为这是自我推销。但是，如果我将其称为“教育您的团队所做的所有伟大工作”呢？为了帮助人们了解为什么你的团队应该获得更多资源，你必须实际分享你所做的事情。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there something that you believe that you think most other people don't believe?
turns.zh: 有没有什么事情是你相信但其他人不相信的？

turns.speaker: Deb Liu
turns.en: The most important career decision you make is who you marry. Is this person lifting you up or pushing you back? You will have a much more successful career if your home life is in balance. It's like a yin and a yang.
turns.zh: 您做出的最重要的职业决定是与谁结婚。这个人是在提升你还是在推你后退？如果你的家庭生活平衡，你的事业将会更加成功。就像阴和阳一样。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Today, my guest is Deb Liu. Deb was VP of product at Facebook where she spent over 11 years and while they're created and led Facebook marketplace, which is now used by over 1 billion people monthly, she also led the development of Facebook's first mobile ad product for apps and its mobile ad network. Also built the company's games business and payments platform, including Facebook Pay. (00:01:23): Prior to Facebook, she was director at both PayPal and eBay. She's on the board of Intuit and for the past three and a half years, she's been the CEO of Ancestry. I actually generally have a rule of no CEOs on this podcast, but to me, Deb is a great exception because she's a product person at heart. In our conversation, Deb shares a ton of tactical career advice, including why resilience is so key to career success, how to PM your career like you PM your product, how to be successful in business as an introvert, what she's learned about building multiple billion dollars zero to one businesses within a large company like Facebook and so much more. (00:01:59): Deb is so full of wisdom and I'm really excited to share her insights with more people. If you enjoy this podcast, don't forget to subscribe and follow it in your favorite podcasting app or YouTube. It's the best way to avoid missing future episodes and helps the podcast tremendously. With that, I bring you Deb Liu. (00:02:18): Deb, thank you so much for being here. Welcome to the podcast.
turns.zh: 今天，我的嘉宾是刘黛玉。 Deb 曾在 Facebook 担任产品副总裁超过 11 年，在创建和领导 Facebook 市场（目前每月有超过 10 亿人使用）的同时，她还领导了 Facebook 首款应用程序移动广告产品及其移动广告网络的开发。还打造了公司的游戏业务和支付平台，包括Facebook Pay。 (00:01:23)：在加入 Facebook 之前，她曾担任 PayPal 和 eBay 的总监。她是 Intuit 的董事会成员，在过去三年半的时间里，她一直担任 Ancestry 的首席执行官。事实上，我通常规定这个播客上没有首席执行官，但对我来说，黛布是一个很大的例外，因为她本质上是一个产品人。在我们的谈话中，Deb 分享了大量的战术性职业建议，包括为什么韧性对于职业成功如此关键、如何像产品经理一样管理你的职业生涯、作为一个内向者如何在商业上取得成功、她在 Facebook 这样的大公司内建立价值数十亿美元的零到一业务的经验等等。 (00:01:59)：黛布充满智慧，我很高兴能与更多人分享她的见解。如果您喜欢这个播客，请不要忘记订阅并在您最喜欢的播客应用程序或 YouTube 中关注它。这是避免错过未来剧集的最佳方式，并且对播客有很大帮助。接下来，我为您带来黛布·刘。 (00:02:18)：黛布，非常感谢你来到这里。欢迎来到播客。

turns.speaker: Deb Liu
turns.en: It's wonderful to be here, Lenny.
turns.zh: 很高兴来到这里，莱尼。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's wonderful to have you here. You have had such an incredible career. You're VP of product at Facebook. You're director at eBay and PayPal. You're on the board of Intuit. You've been the CEO of Ancestry now for the past three and a half years. This is a career path that a lot of people dream of and honestly just like one of those roles is a dream for a lot of people. And so I wanted to start with just this question and I want to see where the conversation takes us. If you could give one specific piece of advice to someone that's looking to do well in their career or to do better in their career based on what has worked well for you, what would that be?
turns.zh: 很高兴你能来到这里。你拥有如此令人难以置信的职业生涯。您是 Facebook 的产品副总裁。您是 eBay 和 PayPal 的总监。您是 Intuit 董事会成员。过去三年半以来，您一直担任 Ancestry 的首席执行官。这是很多人梦想的职业道路，老实说，就像其中一个角色是很多人的梦想一样。所以我想从这个问题开始，我想看看对话将带我们走向何方。如果您可以向那些希望在职业生涯中取得好成绩或希望根据对您来说效果良好的方法在职业生涯中做得更好的人提供一条具体建议，那会是什么？

turns.speaker: Deb Liu
turns.en: Always be learning, and I tell this to everybody, so I often tell people, someone who's always learning is always going to exceed someone who's the expert today. You're going to find people... The one thing about school is that we go to school and there's such a thing as getting a hundred on the test, a perfect score on the SAT, graduating with a 4.0. Well, there's nothing like that in careers, right? We think it's actually a non-linear experience and there's always something better than you at speaking or presenting or strategy or execution. But if you're always learning, learning from the best, getting feedback, you're always going to get better every single day. (00:03:35): And that's what I have always held, which is each job I took, I didn't necessarily qualify for it. I wasn't necessarily the very best at it, and so it became the student of being better at that job. And once I mastered that, I was a student for something else, something else and something else. And so I always balanced learning and impact, which was you can have the most impact, the job you know the best, but then you stop learning. And if you're learning all the time, you're not necessarily having impact. (00:04:00): So how do you keep going back and forth and back and forth so that you're not going straight up a lot or you're actually laddering back and forth into different things where you're having an amazing time where you know everything and then you're the newbie again and learning new things, and you're incorporating what you used to know into what you're learning and the impact that you have today and so on and so forth.
turns.zh: 不断学习，我告诉每个人这一点，所以我经常告诉人们，不断学习的人总是会超过今天的专家。你会找到人……关于学校的一件事就是我们去学校，并且有这样的事情：考试得一百分，SAT 成绩满分，以 4.0 毕业。嗯，职业生涯中没有这样的事，对吧？我们认为这实际上是一种非线性体验，并且在演讲、演示、策略或执行方面总有比您更好的东西。但如果你总是学习，向最好的人学习，获得反馈，你每天都会变得更好。 (00:03:35)：这就是我一直坚持的观点，即我接受的每一份工作，我并不一定有资格胜任。我不一定是最擅长的，所以它成为了在这项工作上做得更好的学生。一旦我掌握了这一点，我就成为了其他东西、其他东西和其他东西的学生。所以我总是平衡学习和影响力，这就是你可以产生最大的影响力，你最了解的工作，但随后你就停止了学习。如果你一直在学习，你不一定会产生影响。 (00:04:00)：那么你如何不断地来来回回，这样你就不会直线上升很多，或者你实际上是在不同的事情上来回走动，在那里你度过了一段美妙的时光，你知道了一切，然后你又成为了新手，学习新的东西，你将你过去知道的东西融入到你正在学习的东西和你今天所产生的影响中，等等。

turns.speaker: Deb Liu
turns.en: We'll start with my career in tech. So I had worked in consulting before business school. I went to Stanford for business school, came out to California, didn't know that much about tech, but I really loved using eBay. So I interned there my first year in business school and then when it came to finding a job, I really wasn't sure what we wanted to do, but we wanted to move back to the East Coast. And so I wasn't looking and I couldn't find a job. I think it was really hard. It was 2002. And so I ran into Tim Wenzel and Catherine Wu. So Catherine Wu was from Airbnb as you might know her. And Tim Wenzel put together the PayPal Mafia. He was the recruiter for PayPal. (00:07:51): Went to this table and I said, "Absolutely love PayPal, use it all the time. I'm a big seller on eBay," and he's like, "Do you want a job?" I'm like, "No, I'm actually going back east. "And he's like, "Just come in and talk to us." And so I said, "Okay. Well, what kind of jobs do you have?" And he's like, "I have jobs in product and I have jobs in marketing." Now, I've taken marketing class obviously in business school, and I said, "I wonder what this other product job is." (00:08:12): So I look over at Catherine and I've seen her around Stanford before, so she was a year ahead of me and I said, "Well, what do you do?" She said, "Product." I'm like, "That sounds good. I'll do that." And that's actually how I fell into product management. Well, I actually, and I'm embarrassed to say faked my way through those interviews, because during the interviews they're like, "Well, what would you build?" And since I was an avid user of both products, I could really richly say, "Here's the product feedback I have. Here are the new products you should build. Here's my feedback on things that we should be doing differently." (00:08:39): And they said, "Congratulations." And they gave me the job. And embarrassingly I went to the first day of work and I said to Amy Clement, who was the VP of product at the time, and I said, "Okay, I literally have no idea what this product job is." (00:08:54): She showed me the ropes and she was so incredible. She actually showed me, she said, "All those ideas you had, all that energy you've had around building these things, we go do that. Let's go do it." And I said, "Well, how do you do that?" And she said, "Well, you write down what you want to build and you work with the engineers to do it." And I just remember thinking, "This is crazy. I have no idea what I'm doing." (00:09:14): It was such an incredible adventure though. Those first few years, I just learned so much about the craft of building, how to really think through product use cases, how to think through what customers wanted, not just the customer of one, myself, but really what true customers and customer cohorts wanted. And so it was really a time when I felt like I was really blossoming, but I didn't come in with mastery. I came with a curiosity and I think that's what made me a great product manager was that I didn't have a set way of doing things. There wasn't some playbook I was trying to play. There wasn't some framework, but instead I was willing to learn.
turns.zh: 我们将从我的科技职业生涯开始。所以我在读商学院之前曾从事咨询工作。我去了斯坦福大学商学院，来到加利福尼亚州，对科技了解不多，但我真的很喜欢使用 eBay。所以我在商学院实习了第一年，然后当谈到找工作时，我真的不确定我们想做什么，但我们想搬回东海岸。所以我没有寻找，也找不到工作。我认为这真的很难。那是 2002 年。于是我遇到了蒂姆·温泽尔 (Tim Wenzel) 和凯瑟琳·吴 (Catherine Wu)。你可能认识 Catherine Wu，她来自 Airbnb。 Tim Wenzel 组建了 PayPal Mafia。他是 PayPal 的招聘人员。 (00:07:51)：走到这张桌子前，我说，“我非常喜欢 PayPal，一直使用它。我是 eBay 上的大卖家，”他说，“你想要一份工作吗？”我说，“不，我实际上要回东部。”他说，“进来和我们谈谈吧。”所以我说，“好吧。那么，你从事什么类型的工作？”他说，“我有产品方面的工作，也有营销方面的工作。”现在，我显然已经在商学院上过营销课程，我说：“我想知道另一个产品工作是什么。” (00:08:12)：所以我看着凯瑟琳，我以前在斯坦福大学见过她，所以她比我早一年，我说，“好吧，你是做什么的？”她说：“产品。”我想，“听起来不错。我会这么做的。”这实际上就是我进入产品管理的过程。嗯，实际上，我很尴尬地说在这些采访中我是假装的，因为在采访中他们会说，“那么，你会构建什么？”由于我是这两种产品的狂热用户，我真的可以很丰富地说，“这是我得到的产品反馈。这是你应该构建的新产品。这是我对我们应该采取不同做法的事情的反馈。” (00:08:39)：他们说：“恭喜。”他们给了我这份工作。令人尴尬的是，我第一天上班时就对当时的产品副总裁艾米·克莱门特 (Amy Clement) 说，“好吧，我真的不知道这个产品工作是什么。” (00:08:54)：她向我展示了秘诀，她太不可思议了。她实际上向我展示了，她说，“你拥有的所有这些想法，你为构建这些东西所拥有的所有能量，我们都去做。让我们去做吧。”我说：“那么，你是怎么做到的呢？”她说：“好吧，你写下你想要构建的东西，然后与工程师一起完成它。”我只记得我当时想：“这太疯狂了。我不知道自己在做什么。” (00:09:14)：但这真是一次令人难以置信的冒险。在最初的几年里，我学到了很多关于构建的技巧，如何真正思考产品用例，如何思考客户想要什么，不仅仅是我自己的客户，而是真正的客户和客户群体想要什么。所以那确实是一个我感觉自己真正绽放的时刻，但我并没有掌握。我带着好奇心来到这里，我认为这让我成为一名出色的产品经理，因为我没有固定的做事方式。我并没有尝试去玩什么剧本。没有什么框架，但我愿意学习。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So one takeaway might be from this, the phrase, fake it till you make it. Any thoughts on just how to... I imagine many people right now are like, "Oh, I'm trying to get a job as a pm. How do I do this? That sounds great. I'm going to pass this interview, figure out the job after I joined."
turns.zh: 因此，这句话的一个要点可能是“假装成功，直到成功”。关于如何……我想现在很多人都会说，“哦，我正在努力找一份下午的工作。我该怎么做？听起来不错。我将通过这次面试，在加入后弄清楚这份工作。”

turns.speaker: Deb Liu
turns.en: Coming in with humbleness was really important, but during the interview process, actually, I didn't realize this, but they asked me questions as if I was a product manager, as if I knew what I was doing. I think when you have passion around a product or passion around a company or around a business model or around something, it shows. And so it's not necessarily faking the enthusiasm or faking the idea that you want to work there, but you don't have to know how to write this spec or PRD or briefings or anything like that. You don't know how to do customer research or do data analytics or read reports, but instead show your passion around the product itself, around the use case, around the customer. (00:10:41): Show who you are and why you care. I think sometimes people just say, "I want a product job." But you have to be able to fall in love with the problem. You have to fall in love, not with the product, but I said the problem, right? The use case. What problem are you trying to solve? And if you can do that, you can be a great product manager even without a lot of experience.
turns.zh: 谦虚地进来确实很重要，但在面试过程中，实际上我没有意识到这一点，但他们问我问题就好像我是产品经理一样，好像我知道自己在做什么。我认为，当你对一种产品、对一家公司、一种商业模式或某件事充满热情时，它就会表现出来。因此，这不一定是假装热情或假装你想在那里工作，但你不必知道如何编写此规范或 PRD 或简报或类似的内容。你不知道如何进行客户研究、数据分析或阅读报告，而是表现出你对产品本身、用例和客户的热情。 (00:10:41)：展示你是谁以及你为什么关心。我想有时人们只是说，“我想要一份产品工作。”但你必须能够爱上这个问题。你必须爱上，而不是爱上产品，但我说的是问题，对吧？用例。您想解决什么问题？如果你能做到这一点，即使没有很多经验，你也可以成为一名出色的产品经理。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's an awesome piece of advice. So just lean into the passion. First of all, part of it is you have to be excited about the thing you're trying to work on or thinking about the company you're thinking about joining. Sounds like that's a prerequisite here. We have a podcast episode with Uri Levine who has a whole book called Fall in Love with the Problem, which is all about that same idea actually for startup founders.
turns.zh: 这是一个很棒的建议。因此，只要投入热情即可。首先，部分原因是你必须对你正在尝试做的事情或考虑你正在考虑加入的公司感到兴奋。听起来这是这里的先决条件。我们有一个由尤里·莱文 (Uri Levine) 主持的播客节目，他写了一整本书，名为《爱上问题》(Fall in Love with the Problem)，这本书实际上是针对初创公司创始人的同样的想法。

turns.speaker: Deb Liu
turns.en: I'll have to read it.
turns.zh: 我得读一下。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, he always wears a shirt, fall in love with the problem, not the solution.
turns.zh: 是的，他总是穿着衬衫，爱上问题，而不是解决方案。

turns.speaker: Deb Liu
turns.en: Yes, is absolutely the most important skill for a product leader.
turns.zh: 是的，这绝对是产品负责人最重要的技能。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Something else I've heard you talk about in terms of something that contributed to your success is being okay with failure and just bouncing back quickly versus avoiding failure. Is that something that you can come back to a lot?
turns.zh: 我听你谈论过一些有助于你成功的事情，那就是接受失败，快速恢复，而不是避免失败。这是你可以经常回来的事情吗？

turns.speaker: Deb Liu
turns.en: Well, here's what I noticed about everybody. I've coached a ton of people in my life. I have managed big teens and the people who are most successful are not the people who had no failures, who were lived charm lives, head up into the right careers and got promoted every cycle. The people who were most successful were the ones who actually through adversity, learned to turn stumbling blocks into stepping stones. They were the ones who got hard feedback and then came back stronger because now they learned what to do differently. (00:12:09): They were the ones who products failed, but they said, "You know what? I'm going to turn this failure into success. I'm going to take those lessons and make this company stronger." When you live a charmed product life, you always work on everything that's easy. You don't actually... Trees are strong because they bend in the wind, because they're tested, because it's cold, because it's windy, because there's conditions. (00:12:31): And that's how a tree goes grow strong and tall over many generations. And I think sometimes we think, "Oh yeah, I wish I lived a charm life." And that is not what we want. You want to have enough adversity that you learn to overcome so that you can build stronger over time and build resilience in your career. (00:12:50): I've seen that so much, which is the best product leaders I ever worked with are the ones that have the toughest stories, that had the hardest feedback, but also the ones who were able to bounce back quickly and make it happen.
turns.zh: 嗯，这就是我对每个人的观察。我一生中指导过很多人。我管理过大青少年，最成功的人并不是那些没有失败过的人，他们过着迷人的生活，进入正确的职业并在每个周期都得到晋升。最成功的人是那些真正经历逆境的人，学会把绊脚石变成垫脚石的人。他们得到了严厉的反馈，然后变得更加强大，因为现在他们学会了如何做不同的事情。 (00:12:09)：他们是产品失败的人，但他们说，“你知道吗？我要把这次失败变成成功。我要吸取这些教训，让这家公司变得更强大。”当你过着迷人的产品生活时，你总是会做一切简单的事情。你实际上并不……树木之所以坚强，是因为它们在风中弯曲，因为它们经过了考验，因为天气寒冷，因为有风，因为有条件。 (00:12:31)：这就是一棵树如何在许多世代中变得坚强、高大的原因。我想有时我们会想，“哦，是的，我希望我过着迷人的生活。”这不是我们想要的。你希望有足够多的逆境来学习克服，这样你就能随着时间的推移变得更强大，并在你的职业生涯中建立韧性。 (00:12:50)：我见过很多这样的情况，与我共事过的最好的产品领导者是那些拥有最艰难的故事、最艰难的反馈的人，但也是那些能够快速恢复并实现目标的人。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: We have a segment on this podcast called Failure Corner where people share a failure they went through kind of along the same lines and something we learned from that experience. Is there an example of that from your career where a failure made you stronger?
turns.zh: 我们在这个播客上有一个名为“失败角落”的部分，人们分享他们经历过的类似失败以及我们从这次经历中学到的东西。在你的职业生涯中，有没有失败让你变得更坚强的例子？

turns.speaker: Deb Liu
turns.en: Yeah. I remember there was a job that I really wanted at Facebook and I'd been there for a long time. I had been leading different teams. I was a VP of product and then GM. There was one job that I never got to do, so I got to do all the jobs I wanted and Mark gave it to someone else. I told him at the time when he gave it to the first person who was amazing at it, I said, "If this job were open, I'd like to be considered for it." (00:13:37): The job opened up later, gave it to someone else. And I said to Mark, again, "I really wanted that job." And he said, "Not only will I not give you that job, you'll never have that job at this company."
turns.zh: 是的。我记得 Facebook 有一份我非常想要的工作，而且我已经在那里工作了很长时间。我一直在领导不同的团队。我曾担任产品副总裁，然后担任总经理。有一项工作我从来没有做过，所以我必须做我想做的所有工作，而马克把它交给了别人。当他把这份工作交给第一个在这方面表现出色的人时，我告诉他，“如果这份工作有空缺，我希望被考虑。” (00:13:37)：这个工作后来空出来了，给了别人。我再次对马克说：“我真的很想要那份工作。”他说：“我不仅不会给你那份工作，而且你永远不会在这家公司得到这份工作。”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What?
turns.zh: 什么？

turns.speaker: Deb Liu
turns.en: He didn't say it harshly. But he was giving me feedback about something which he did not see me in that role, in a role that I really wanted. And I had to decide each time like, "What do I do with this information?" This is my dream job. Actually, I decided I was going to turn the job I had and the job I wanted, and that's a choice. I could have said, you know what? I can't have that job. I could go do something else, but I didn't. I took the job I had with the team I had and I turned it into this thing that was going to be something we wanted. (00:14:20): And so I think sometimes it's not... I think that that experience was a very humbling experience because to be told no and then to say that this will never happen was really hard. But at the same time it was a reminder that you're not right for every job even if you think you are. And that you can take the raw materials of what you have and turn it into what you want.
turns.zh: 他说得并不严厉。但他给了我一些反馈，但他没有看到我扮演那个角色，一个我真正想要的角色。我每次都必须做出决定，比如“我该如何处理这些信息？”这是我梦想的工作。事实上，我决定要改变我现有的工作和我想要的工作，这是一个选择。我本可以说，你知道吗？我不能得到那份工作。我本来可以去做点别的事，但我没有。我接受了我和我的团队的工作，并将其变成了我们想要的东西。 (00:14:20)：所以我认为有时并不是......我认为那次经历是一次非常令人谦卑的经历，因为被告知不，然后又说这永远不会发生真的很难。但同时它也提醒我们，即使你认为自己适合所有工作，但你并不适合所有工作。你可以利用你所拥有的原材料并将其变成你想要的东西。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Are you able to share what those jobs were that you wanted to get that you never got?
turns.zh: 你能分享一下那些你想得到但却从未得到过的工作吗？

turns.speaker: Deb Liu
turns.en: I never actually shared it publicly, but it's something which I had always had a role where I did new things for the company and there was a role where it was running something which more of an existing business, but I had always been kind of the innovator, the new stuff person. I had taken over so many new things. And so maybe that wasn't the right thing at the right time for me, but it was something that was really incredible and a turning point for me.
turns.zh: 我实际上从未公开分享过它，但我一直扮演着一个角色，为公司做新事物，还有一个角色是运营更多现有业务，但我一直是创新者，新事物的人。我接手了很多新事物。所以也许这对我来说不是在正确的时间发生的正确的事情，但这对我来说确实是令人难以置信的转折点。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Great segue to an area I wanted to spend some time on which is building zero to one stuff within a larger company. So from what I can tell you built 2 billion businesses within a large company, Facebook marketplace, and then the ads platform within Facebook and maybe more. I don't know, the payments stuff, the games. I don't know. Maybe there's billions of dollars there I don't even know about. And this is very rare and very hard, and it's something we talk a little bit on this podcast, just the skills to build something new. (00:15:38): I know with marketplace it was not something people believed in for a long time. It took a lot of work to convince people to actually give it a shot. So I guess the question here is just what have you found are key tactics to start something new and allow it to continue to exist and get to a place where people start to believe it? What has worked for you?
turns.zh: 很好地延续了我想花一些时间在一家大公司内构建从零到一的东西的领域。因此，据我所知，您在一家大公司、Facebook 市场、然后 Facebook 内的广告平台甚至更多方面建立了 20 亿个业务。我不知道，支付的东西，游戏。我不知道。也许那里有数十亿美元我什至不知道。这是非常罕见和非常困难的，这是我们在这个播客上谈论的一些内容，只是构建新事物的技能。 (00:15:38)：我知道人们长期以来并不相信市场。说服人们真正尝试一下需要做很多工作。所以我想这里的问题是你发现了什么是开始新事物并允许它继续存在并达到人们开始相信它的地方的关键策略？什么对你有用？

turns.speaker: Deb Liu
turns.en: So first, I didn't build the ads platform. I actually built the first direct response ad product company ever had. But we'll talk about how that led to why direct response is a vast majority of the ads revenue for the company. But one thing that it was really interesting is that I really saw my opportunity in Facebook to be somebody that zigged when other people zagged. There were amazing people who did a lot of the really core products working on feed, photos, videos. (00:16:25): I came in actually on the payments team and we worked on payments and eventually built games, which was the first billion dollar business. It was very successful. We worked with the likes of all the game companies that were on the Canvas games platform. And it was just an incredible opportunity to start from scratch and built something really cool. We built Facebook credits, which eventually became the Facebook payment system. (00:16:47): And then from there on I built the first direct response ads product. And again, leveraging the skills that we had, we had a lot of relationships with game companies because of my time and payments. And so we just said, "Hey look, what ad product do you want?" And they said, "Actually, your biggest challenge is the shift to mobile. Build us a mobile acquisition engine." And we said, "That's doable." (00:17:09): At the time the company was very brand oriented. Most of the ads... Actually almost all the ads on the platform were brand and we were not even on the ads team. So we actually worked on this team called the platform team. We said, "Okay, we'll build an ads product for the Facebook feed, the new mobile Facebook feed." And suddenly it became a billion dollar business within about 18 months, which was such an incredible journey. (00:17:30): We worked on the mobile advertising platform, so basically the mobile ads network. That was a great experience. And so each time I worked on something, it was just... The thing that you have to remember is the failure rate for something like this is very high. You start something and the amount of iteration... People think, "Oh yeah, it's easy." You start something and it's linear because you have all the resources of this company behind you. But actually everything in the company is like, "Let's do the most important thing." (00:17:58): These are seeds and we'll just let them... And so if you do that, you have to know that you don't get a lot of resources, you get a lot of attention. And I appreciated that because I think I work best when people aren't... There is not a lot of scrutiny. I think sometimes large companies, they say, "Well this innovation team," and then they check in on them way too much. They're like, "Week to week progress, where are you going? What's your strategy?" But so much as you know of building something new is the iteration process. It's the failing a lot. (00:18:27): We actually tested five or six versions of the ads product before we got it to take off and it took months, and then we were on the verge of death multiple times. In fact, I actually went back to run the payments team while I was working on that product because the team we had gathered still want to continue working on it, but I needed a second job back on the payments team because they asked me, "We don't think this thing is going to work. You should go run your old team again." And I thought, "Well, I will do both." (00:18:52): And so I did both for a while until it really took off. The thing that I think a lot of large companies don't realize is that you can love something to death. And so with every new product, I'd rather do it out of the limelight, do it with the minimal resources and have the freedom to fail because success and failure really is... In startups, failing fast is really important or succeeding fast. (00:19:18): It's the long slog that makes it really hard. In a company, you end up getting cut if you're the long slog product. And so being able to just say, "You know what? We're pruning this. We're doing the next thing, the next thing." And then having the time to iterate and grow is really critical.
turns.zh: 所以首先，我没有建立广告平台。我实际上建立了第一家直接响应广告产品公司。但我们将讨论这如何导致直接响应占公司广告收入的绝大多数。但真正有趣的一件事是，我确实在 Facebook 中看到了自己的机会，成为一个在其他人摇摆不定时摇摆不定的人。有一些了不起的人开发了很多真正核心的产品，包括信息流、照片、视频。 (00:16:25)：我实际上加入了支付团队，我们致力于支付并最终开发了游戏，这是第一个十亿美元的业务。这是非常成功的。我们与 Canvas 游戏平台上的所有游戏公司合作。这是一个从头开始并构建一些非常酷的东西的绝佳机会。我们建立了 Facebook 积分，最终成为 Facebook 支付系统。 (00:16:47)：从那时起，我构建了第一个直接响应广告产品。再次，利用我们拥有的技能，由于我的时间和报酬，我们与游戏公司建立了很多关系。所以我们只是说，“嘿，看看，你想要什么广告产品？”他们说：“实际上，您最大的挑战是转向移动。为我们构建一个移动获取引擎。”我们说：“这是可行的。” (00:17:09)：当时公司非常注重品牌。大多数广告......实际上平台上几乎所有广告都是品牌广告，而我们甚至不是广告团队的成员。所以我们实际上在这个称为平台团队的团队中工作。我们说，“好吧，我们将为 Facebook feed 构建一个广告产品，即新的移动 Facebook feed。”在大约 18 个月内，它突然变成了价值 10 亿美元的业务，这是一段令人难以置信的旅程。 (00:17:30)：我们致力于移动广告平台，所以基本上是移动广告网络。那是一次很棒的经历。所以每次我做某事时，只是……你必须记住的是，这样的事情的失败率非常高。你开始做某事并进行大量迭代......人们会想，“哦，是的，这很容易。”你开始做某事，它是线性的，因为你有这家公司的所有资源支持。但实际上公司里的一切都像是“让我们做最重要的事情吧”。 (00:17:58)：这些是种子，我们会让它们...所以如果你这样做，你必须知道你不会获得很多资源，你会得到很多关注。我很欣赏这一点，因为我认为当人们不……没有太多审查时我工作得最好。我认为有时大公司会说，“好吧，这个创新团队”，然后他们对他们的检查太多了。他们会问，“每周都在进步，你要去哪里？你的策略是什么？”但正如您所知道的，构建新事物就是迭代过程。这是很多失败的事情。 (00:18:27)：我们实际上测试了五六个版本的广告产品才让它成功，花了几个月的时间，然后我们多次处于死亡边缘。事实上，当我在开发该产品时，我实际上回去管理支付团队，因为我们聚集的团队仍然想继续开发它，但我需要在支付团队中找到第二份工作，因为他们问我，“我们认为这件事不会起作用。你应该再次管理你的旧团队。”我想：“好吧，我两样都会做。” (00:18:52)：所以我都做了一段时间，直到它真正起飞。我认为很多大公司都没有意识到，你可以热爱某样东西至死不渝。因此，对于每一个新产品，我宁愿在众人瞩目的情况下完成它，用最少的资源完成它，并有失败的自由，因为成功和失败确实是……在初创公司中，快速失败或快速成功非常重要。 (00:19:18)：漫长的过程让它变得非常困难。在公司里，如果你是长期苦干的产品，你最终会被裁掉。因此，我们可以说：“你知道吗？我们正在修剪这个。我们正在做下一件事，下一件事。”然后，有时间进行迭代和成长非常重要。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So as a leader trying to do this and create space for this, is there something you've learned about how to allow for, "Don't over scrutinize us, don't look at us too carefully. We don't want to be in the limelight. Don't put too many resources on this yet." Is it just like, "Hey, Mark. Here's what I think." I imagine it's not as easy as that. There's a lot of influence and that kind of work. Is there any tactics that you could share to create this sort of environment?
turns.zh: 因此，作为一个试图做到这一点并为此创造空间的领导者，您是否已经学会了如何允许“不要过度审视我们，不要太仔细地审视我们。我们不想成为众人瞩目的焦点。暂时不要在这方面投入太多资源。”是不是就像，“嘿，马克。这就是我的想法。”我想这并不那么容易。有很多影响力和类似的工作。您可以分享一些创建这种环境的策略吗？

turns.speaker: Deb Liu
turns.en: I think the most important part of the environment is really patience. And again, this is a portfolio strategy and I tell every PM who... I used to do a new hire PM class and I say, "Look, a lot of you are going to go into the core product and your job is to grow X by 3 to 5% every six months. Growing engagement or growing sessions or maybe growing video views or whatever your metric is, you're trying to grow something 5% and then you exceed expectations." (00:20:27): And I said, "And then a bunch of you are like, 'I want to do something new. I want to build something from scratch.'" And I said, "By the way, a very, very successful company for a new set of products has a 50% hit rate. So half of you are going to come back in a year and have a different job because that did not work out. Do you have the resilience to do that?" And I think somebody, you enter a large company... By the way, you can have an amazing career building core products because that is an incredible journey within... Because you learn so much about the mechanics of what that takes. (00:20:59): And yet at the same time, I found a lot of energy from doing something that someone hasn't done before. And so I really enjoyed the, "Hey, this thing could fail. Let's pivot. Let's try to figure out. Let's prune this. Let's try that." And not everything I did there succeeded, but a lot of the things that are the lasting products are once that gotten really big. And so for me it was a greater reward and it made a journey so much more interesting. (00:21:24): But for others, I think work on the core product, learn the skills. It is absolutely respectable as well. But if you choose to be the person who works on innovation new products, expect in a year, you might literally have nothing to show for it, but the lessons that you learned. And I think those lessons are really precious and we often underestimate that too.
turns.zh: 我认为环境中最重要的部分是真正的耐心。再说一遍，这是一个投资组合策略，我告诉每一位 PM，我曾经在新员工 PM 课程中说过，“看，你们中的很多人都会进入核心产品，你们的工作是每六个月增长 X 3% 到 5%。增加参与度或增加会话，或者增加视频观看次数或无论您的指标是什么，您都试图增长 5%，然后您就超出了预期。” (00:20:27)：我说，“然后你们中的一群人会说，‘我想做一些新的事情。我想从头开始构建一些东西。’”我说，“顺便说一句，一家非常非常成功的公司生产一套新产品，其命中率为 50%。所以，你们中的一半人会在一年后回来，做一份不同的工作，因为那没有成功。你们有能力做到这一点吗？”我认为有人，你进入一家大公司......顺便说一句，你可以在构建核心产品方面拥有令人惊叹的职业生涯，因为这是一段令人难以置信的旅程......因为你学到了很多关于它所需要的机制。 (00:20:59)：但与此同时，我从做别人从未做过的事情中发现了很多能量。所以我真的很喜欢这样的说法：“嘿，这件事可能会失败。让我们转向。让我们尝试找出答案。让我们修剪这个。让我们尝试一下。”并不是我在那里所做的一切都成功了，但很多持久的产品都是曾经变得非常大的。所以对我来说这是一个更大的奖励，它让旅程变得更加有趣。 (00:21:24)：但对于其他人来说，我认为致力于核心产品，学习技能。这也是绝对值得尊敬的。但如果你选择成为致力于创新新产品的人，预计一年后，你可能实际上没有什么可展示的，但你学到了教训。我认为这些教训非常宝贵，但我们也常常低估了这一点。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Along those lines, do you think it's a good career move to do a zero to one thing within a bigger company? Or is it often a bad idea? Do you have any advice there for folks?
turns.zh: 沿着这些思路，你认为在一家更大的公司里做从零到一的事情是一个很好的职业转变吗？或者这通常是一个坏主意？您对人们有什么建议吗？

turns.speaker: Deb Liu
turns.en: It depends. It depends on your personality in the company. So the one thing I realized about my role was that I did a lot of... I had five different careers at the company over 11 years. And so most people don't realize that when you work on new things, you're constantly adding to your portfolio, subtracting from it, growing things, pruning them. And so you could just work on so many cool things except everything has similar... It's like it rhymes, but it's not exactly the same. (00:22:19): So you learn the lessons of how to get things done, how to get resource, how to get support when the product is not working, how to not get prunes in the next culling. And those are really, really important skills. But I think for people who are just starting out of the career, it is a very high risk thing to do. So if you're very early in the career, I encourage people just learn the core skills first. You can learn the core skills when there's a lot of stability. This product is growing X percent, like 5%, and you're going to grow at 10. That's amazing. (00:22:47): That is because you are there, you're going to change your trajectory of the product, or this thing has a hundred thousand users, you're going to get it to 200,000. Those are the kinds of things that are going to be successful for you and you can put on your resume. But I think it reaches a point in your career where you have to decide, when am I going to take the big swing? Because the big swings are the things that you write your career stories about. They're not just, I moved this metric X, but I changed your trajectory in this way. (00:23:17): And so the big swings though have a lot of failures along the way. And so you have to understand you're making trade-offs in that. I encourage everybody to take some time, two, three years in their career when they're ready for the big swing, where if it doesn't work... If it works, you run the team, you run this amazing product. It doesn't work, you can always go back and go back to the core products.
turns.zh: 这取决于。这取决于你在公司的性格。因此，关于我的角色，我意识到的一件事是，我做了很多……11 年来，我在公司从事过 5 种不同的职业。因此，大多数人没有意识到，当你从事新事物时，你会不断地在你的投资组合中添加、减去、种植、修剪它们。所以你可以做很多很酷的事情，除了一切都有相似之处……就像押韵一样，但并不完全相同。 (00:22:19)：所以你会学到如何把事情做好，如何获得资源，如何在产品不起作用时获得支持，如何在下一次淘汰中不被修剪。这些都是非常非常重要的技能。但我认为对于刚刚开始职业生涯的人来说，这是一件风险非常高的事情。因此，如果您处于职业生涯的早期，我鼓励人们首先学习核心技能。当有很大的稳定性时，你可以学习核心技能。这个产品正在增长 X%，比如 5%，而你将增长 10%。这太神奇了。 (00:22:47)：那是因为你在那里，你要改变你的产品轨迹，或者这个东西有十万用户，你要把它增加到20万。这些都是对你来说会成功的事情，你可以把它写在你的简历上。但我认为，在你的职业生涯中，你必须做出决定，我什么时候要采取重大举措？因为大波动是你写职业故事的内容。他们不仅仅是，我移动了这个指标X，而且我以这种方式改变了你的轨迹。 (00:23:17)：尽管如此，大的波动一路上也有很多失败。所以你必须明白你正在为此做出权衡。我鼓励每个人在他们的职业生涯中花一些时间，两三年，当他们准备好迎接大转变时，如果它不起作用……如果它起作用，你就可以管理团队，你就可以运行这个令人惊叹的产品。实在不行，你可以随时返回，回到核心产品。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's interesting how your strategy here is very similar to a product portfolio strategy where as a team should have a few big bets and then a lot of incremental stuff. And it reminds me about this awesome post called You Are in Control of Your Career. And the argument in your post is you should PM your career the way you PM your product. So there's a lot of synergy here. So maybe just diving into this post and advice around this, how should someone be PMing their career, the way they PM a product? What's your take there?
turns.zh: 有趣的是，你的策略与产品组合策略非常相似，作为一个团队应该有一些大的赌注，然后是很多增量的东西。这让我想起了一篇很棒的文章，名为“你的职业生涯由你掌控”。你帖子中的论点是你应该像PM产品一样PM你的职业生涯。所以这里有很多协同作用。因此，也许只是深入研究这篇文章并就此提出建议，人们应该如何PM他们的职业生涯，他们PM产品的方式？你对此有何看法？

turns.speaker: Deb Liu
turns.en: By the way, for your PM audience, I want to say this, which is a lot of the greatest PMs are the worst PMs of their careers. They love products. They love the crafts. They love the customer research, the data. They have plans, they have timelines. And then when it comes to career, they have none of those things. They just drift from job to job. "Hey, should I take this role or this role? How do I think about this?" But if I said you had to write a spec for your career, what's in there? What are your milestones? What are the skills? What are the features that you want to have of your career? How are you going to get there? What does success look like? (00:24:41): You actually have metrics for your product, and yet you don't have metrics for your career. I coach a lot of people and when I coach them, I ask them, "Well, where do you want to see yourself in five years? Where do you want to go?" And half the people have no idea. I think that's really tragic because when you PM your career, it's about intentionality. But I'll tell you the story of my career and how I was the accidental PM and then eventually... I told you how I accidentally fell into PM, but also fell into so many of the things that happened in my PM career. (00:25:10): And if I had to go back, I would think much more deeply about what I want to accomplish. So I ended up at PayPal working for a guy named Dave Lee who reported to Amy Clement, and then he left. And so she offered me his role. I had only managed people for, I don't know, 15 seconds. I was two years out of business school and I was definitely not qualified to do his job. He was the director of product. I wasn't even a director and I was running the team for eBay. (00:25:34): So basically the PayPal part of eBay, which was basically half the company's revenues and profits. Totally unqualified. I ended up in this job and I do a good job. I ended up doing it for several years. I built up the team and we have a great relationship with eBay. Our team was very close and we were able to actually build something really lasting that worked really well. And then I had a baby. And so this happens in a lot of women's careers. I was turning 30, I had my son, and I had to leave for six months. (00:26:08): So I handed my product to my successor, Mike Woo and he ended up taking over. He did such a good job while I was gone, I didn't want to displace him when I got back. And so I thought, "Well, I'll go and look for another role." I couldn't really find a product role I liked, I mean, because there weren't that many product director roles. And so I ended up in corporate strategy. So I worked for the amazing Rajiv who was CEO at the time. He since passed and I wrote his speeches, worked on strategies, I worked on digital goods and charity, and ended up building that into a vertical for the company. So charity, social commerce and digital goods. (00:26:40): And I thought, "Okay, this is an interesting job." So I create the job, have a couple product managers, wasn't really sure where this was going, and then one day I was like, "You know what? I'm not feeling this. I have a child at home." I had gotten into what Cheryl Sandberg calls that kind of between kids situation where I was bored of my job. (00:26:59): I was working one of the VPs I worked with and I resigned. I said, "I'm leaving tech, just I'm going to stay home and maybe start something small." He convinced me to hold off and he said, I'll find you a job. He calls me a week later and he said, "Found you a job with Stephanie Tilenius leading the buyer experience at eBay product." And I said, "Oh, that sounds interesting." So I said, "Sure, as you notice, I do not have a plan. I'm just drifting. I'm so fortunate that I had amazing mentors who gave me opportunities, but end up working for Greg Fant and Stephanie Tilenius at eBay for two years. (00:27:34): I led the buyer experience. We did some really good work there. And then went on maternity leave again. And I get a call from a friend, my old engineering manager from PayPal, "Hey, I'm at Facebook. Do you want to come? You can't come into product. You need a CS degree for that, but we have a product marketing job open." I was like, "Sounds good." Drop into Facebook. And so again, no idea what I'm doing back in product marketing. So I spent a few years doing that. Eventually was invited into product and so on and so forth. (00:28:02): And each job that came along was organic, but also kind of accidental. I see that happen in a lot of careers, which is my story when you look back, looks great. It looks like it all worked out, but I had almost zero intentionality in any of these. And I think that had I had more agency and I thought about what I wanted, I could actually measure is this the thing that would get me further or not? (00:28:24): I ended up extremely lucky, but not everybody does. And so I think having a plan allows you to compare every decision. It's not like when you're offered an admission to college, we're looking at three different offers maybe with financial aid or not, and you can make a decision, "Oh, they're offering me this department, but I can't get into this department." This is how far it is from home. But jobs and roles or nothing like that. Someone calls you one day, "Hey, I'm at Facebook. Do you want to come? I'm actually on maternity leave." And he's like, "Just come talk to me." I'm like, "Why not." (00:29:00): And you end up dropping into different parts of your life and I think sometimes by saying, "Here's where I want to go and here's how I want to get there," you can have such a better career. And so I do encourage everybody to do this and to think about what does success look like in five years and how far am I from that and am I heading in the right direction?
turns.zh: 顺便说一句，对于你们的 PM 听众，我想说的是，很多最伟大的 PM 都是他们职业生涯中最糟糕的 PM。他们热爱产品。他们热爱手工艺品。他们喜欢客户研究和数据。他们有计划，有时间表。而当谈到职业生涯时，他们什么都没有。他们只是从一个工作转移到另一个工作。 “哎，我该接这个角色还是这个角色？我怎么想这个？”但如果我说你必须为你的职业生涯写一份规范，那里面有什么？你的里程碑是什么？有什么技巧？您希望自己的职业生涯具备哪些特点？你要怎么去那里？成功是什么样的？ (00:24:41)：你实际上有产品的指标，但你的职业却没有指标。我指导过很多人，当我指导他们时，我会问他们：“五年后你想看到自己在哪里？你想去哪里？”一半的人不知道。我认为这真的很悲惨，因为当你PM你的职业生涯时，这是关于意图的。但我会告诉你我的职业生涯的故事，以及我如何意外成为 PM，然后最终......我告诉你我如何意外地成为 PM，而且也陷入了我 PM 职业生涯中发生的许多事情。 (00:25:10)：如果我必须回去，我会更深入地思考我想要实现的目标。所以我最终在 PayPal 为一个名叫 Dave Lee 的人工作，他向 Amy Clement 汇报，然后他离开了。所以她给了我他的角色。我只管理了员工 15 秒，我不知道。我已经从商学院毕业两年了，我绝对没有资格做他的工作。他是产品总监。我什至不是董事，但我负责管理 eBay 的团队。 (00:25:34)：基本上是 eBay 的 PayPal 部分，基本上是公司收入和利润的一半。完全没有资格。我最终得到了这份工作并且做得很好。我最终做了几年。我组建了这个团队，我们与 eBay 有着良好的关系。我们的团队非常紧密，我们能够真正构建出真正持久且效果良好的东西。然后我生了孩子。因此，这种情况发生在很多女性的职业生涯中。我已经 30 岁了，有了儿子，我不得不离开六个月。 (00:26:08)：所以我把我的产品交给了我的继任者 Mike Woo，他最终接手了。我不在的时候他做得很好，我回来后不想取代他。所以我想，“好吧，我去寻找另一个角色。”我的意思是，我找不到真正喜欢的产品角色，因为产品总监的角色并不多。所以我最终选择了公司战略。所以我为当时担任首席执行官的出色的拉吉夫工作。他去世后，我写了他的演讲，制定了战略，我研究了数字产品和慈善事业，最终将其打造为公司的垂直领域。慈善事业、社交商务和数字产品也是如此。 (00:26:40)：我想，“好吧，这是一项有趣的工作。”所以我创造了一份工作，有几个产品经理，不太确定这会发生什么，然后有一天我想，“你知道吗？我没有这种感觉。我家里有一个孩子。”我陷入了谢丽尔·桑德伯格（Cheryl Sandberg）所说的那种孩子之间的情况，我对自己的工作感到厌倦。 (00:26:59)：我曾与一位副总裁一起工作，但我辞职了。我说：“我要离开科技行业，只是待在家里，也许可以开始一些小事情。”他说服我推迟，并说，我会给你找一份工作。一周后，他给我打电话，说：“为你找到了一份工作，由 Stephanie Tilenius 领导 eBay 产品的买家体验。”我说：“哦，这听起来很有趣。”所以我说，“当然，正如你所注意到的，我没有计划。我只是随波逐流。我很幸运，我有很棒的导师，他们给了我机会，但最终在 eBay 为 Greg Fant 和 Stephanie Tilenius 工作了两年。(00:27:34)：我领导了买家体验。我们在那里做了一些非常好的工作。然后再次休产假。我接到朋友的电话，他是我以前在 PayPal 的工程经理，“嘿，我在 Facebook。你想来吗？你不能进入产品领域。你需要拥有计算机科学学位，但我们有一个产品营销职位空缺。”我当时想，“听起来不错。”进入 Facebook。再说一次，我不知道我在产品营销方面做了什么。所以我花了几年时间来做这件事。最终被邀请参与产品等等。 (00:28:02)：每项工作都是有机的，但也有点偶然。我看到这种情况发生在很多职业中，这就是我的故事，当你回头看时，看起来很棒。看起来一切都顺利了，但我对这些的意向几乎为零。我认为如果我有更多的代理权并且我思考了我想要什么，我实际上可以衡量这是否会让我走得更远？ (00:28:24)：我最终非常幸运，但并不是每个人都如此。所以我认为制定计划可以让你比较每个决定。这不像当你被大学录取时，我们正在考虑三个不同的录取通知书，可能有经济援助，也可能没有，你可以做出决定，“哦，他们给我提供了这个部门，但我不能进入这个部门。”这就是离家有多远。但工作和角色或者类似的东西都没有。有一天，有人打电话给你，“嘿，我在 Facebook。你想来吗？我实际上正在休产假。”他就像是，“过来跟我说话吧。”我想，“为什么不呢。” (00:29:00)：你最终会进入生活的不同部分，我想有时通过说，“这就是我想去的地方，这就是我想要到达那里的方式”，你可以拥有更好的职业生涯。因此，我确实鼓励每个人都这样做，并思考五年后成功会是什么样子，我离成功还有多远，我是否正朝着正确的方向前进？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What's interesting is I also had a similar path to you where I had zero plan or intention or goal and also just follow things and things worked out. I wonder how often that happens and I wonder if this idea of having intention and planning a roadmap is something you do if things aren't working out because maybe there's some good to not overthinking it and just following pull. I don't know.
turns.zh: 有趣的是，我也有与你类似的道路，我的计划、意图或目标为零，也只是遵循事情和结果。我想知道这种情况多久发生一次，我想知道如果事情没有进展，你是否会采取这种有意图和规划路线图的想法，因为也许不过度思考并只是跟随拉动会有一些好处。我不知道。

turns.speaker: Deb Liu
turns.en: Well, I think the problem is this with you and me, Lenny, is that hindsight bias is a problem. We made it because we weren't intentional in a lot of ways, but for how many people, is that true? For how many people who aren't... You don't have a plan and you get there. I always tell people, if you are sure what your destination is, that's definitely where you're going to end up. But if you actually aim in the right direction, you can shape your learnings, you can shape your roles you take, you can shape your skills towards the place that you want to go.
turns.zh: 好吧，我认为问题在于你和我，莱尼，事后偏见是一个问题。我们之所以能做到这一点，是因为我们在很多方面都不是故意的，但对于多少人来说，这是真的吗？对于有多少人来说……你没有计划，但你就到达了那里。我总是告诉人们，如果你确定你的目的地是什么，那肯定就是你最终要去的地方。但如果你确实瞄准了正确的方向，你就可以塑造你的学习，你可以塑造你所扮演的角色，你可以塑造你的技能，以实现你想去的地方。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: When you talk about getting this offer from Facebook, usually those are like you have three days to decide.
turns.zh: 当你谈论从 Facebook 获得此优惠时，通常你有三天的时间来决定。

turns.speaker: Deb Liu
turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And it feels like that's when the things you've done ahead of time of here's what I want would be most helpful.
turns.zh: 感觉那时你在我想要的事情之前所做的事情将是最有帮助的。

turns.speaker: Deb Liu
turns.en: Also, I think the thing about job opportunities in particular is they tend to come serially. It's only you presented these offers. It's like one role is so different from another and they often don't happen at the same time. They might say, "Well, you have to decide in two weeks." And then you say, "Well, there's this other company I'm talking to and you get a lot of pressure to say yes to this versus this." (00:30:49): And to really having a measuring stick is this getting me closer or further away from where I go? Can allow you to actually take serial decision making to a place where you're measuring against a long-term goal.
turns.zh: 另外，我认为工作机会尤其是它们往往是连续出现的。这些优惠只是您提供的。就好像一个角色与另一个角色如此不同，而且它们通常不会同时发生。他们可能会说：“好吧，你必须在两周内做出决定。”然后你说：“嗯，我正在和另一家公司交谈，你会面临很大的压力，要接受这家公司，而不是接受这家公司。” (00:30:49)：真正有一把尺子会让我离我要去的地方更近还是更远？可以让您真正做出系列决策，以衡量长期目标。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I did a meditation retreat once and when you're meditating, there's this kind of guidance of don't try too hard, don't push yourself to go into a direction, "Oh, I'm not doing a good job. I need to get to this enlightened state." And instead their advice is just push your cart in a direction and think about that's the direction you want head, but you don't need to grasp on to here's where I need to land, here's where I need to go. And I wonder if just having a thought of here's where I want my career to go. I want to be on boards in the future. I want to start a company in the future. I want to become a designer in the future. At least start there maybe just like a direction that you're heading.
turns.zh: 我曾经做过一次冥想静修，当你冥想的时候，有这样的指导，不要太努力，不要强迫自己进入一个方向，“哦，我做得不好。我需要达到这种开悟的状态。”相反，他们的建议是将你的购物车推向一个方向，并考虑那是你想要的方向，但你不需要抓住这是我需要着陆的地方，这是我需要去的地方。我想知道，仅仅想到这里是否就是我想要的职业发展方向。我想将来加入董事会。我将来想开一家公司。我将来想成为一名设计师。至少从那里开始，也许就像你前进的方向一样。

turns.speaker: Deb Liu
turns.en: Yeah. There's a woman who I worked with in product and now she's the founder, very successful founder, and she said to me, "I want to join the board of this Fortune 100 company." She told me the company, and I said, "Okay, that's a lot." So she said, "How can I get there?" And I said, "First, it's probably going to take you 10 years because look at who's on the board. I happen to know a couple people on the board." And I said, "Why don't I introduce you to one of them? And they can tell you how to get there. (00:32:04): But the point is she knew where she wanted to go and she said, "I'm willing to take it first step today." And I said, "First, you've never been on a board. You were very successful, but this is not... There's so many steps before you get there. It's like before you go to Harvard, you have to graduate from elementary school to middle school. You have to take the SAT, you have to apply. I said, "Let's start from the first step and let's break this problem down." (00:32:29): But I love that she knew where she wanted to go and she's like, "Even if I don't make it there, I'll be happier having made this journey." And I love that for her. And I think she's still earlier in her career, she has so much time ahead of her, but it's really incredible to see her kind of on this path and to know that that's her dream, and that I can help her a little bit along the way.
turns.zh: 是的。有一位与我一起从事产品工作的女性，现在她是创始人，非常成功的创始人，她对我说，“我想加入这家财富 100 强公司的董事会。”她告诉我公司的情况，我说：“好吧，就这么多了。”于是她说：“我怎样才能到达那里？”我说：“首先，这可能需要 10 年的时间，因为看看董事会中有哪些人。我碰巧认识董事会中的几个人。”我说，“我为什么不向你介绍其中一个？他们可以告诉你如何到达那里。(00:32:04)：但关键是她知道她想去哪里，她说，“我愿意今天迈出第一步。”我说，“首先，你从未加入过董事会。你非常成功，但这并不是......在你到达那里之前还有很多步骤。就像你去哈佛之前，你必须从小学到初中毕业一样。你必须参加SAT考试，你必须申请。我说：“我们从第一步开始，把这个问题分解一下。” (00:32:29)：但我喜欢她知道自己想去哪里，她会说，“即使我没能到达那里，我会更高兴完成了这次旅程。”我喜欢她这一点。我认为她还处于职业生涯的早期阶段，她还有很多时间，但看到她走上这条道路并知道那是她的梦想，而且我可以一路帮助她，这真是令人难以置信。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It also relates very much to your idea of thinking of your career like a PM thinks about their product where one of the tactics is to imagine the ideal scenario and work backwards from that versus incrementally what's the next thing? What's the next thing? So in this case, she was thinking, "Here's where I want to head. Okay, what's the next thing to get to that direction?" I love that. (00:33:07): This episode is brought to you by Webflow. We're all friends here, so let's be real for a second. We all know that your website shouldn't be a static asset. It should be a dynamic part of your strategy that drives conversions. That's business 101, but here's a number for you. 54% of leaders say web updates take too long. (00:33:53): Okay, going a slightly different direction, I'd say the post that you've written that has most resonated with me was about introverts and how hard it is to be successful as an introvert, and that basically have to learn to be an extrovert as an introvert because in business extroverts are most valued. Can you just talk about of your insight, what you've seen around this and how and your advice to introverts like me about how to be successful in business, what you need to change?
turns.zh: 这也与你思考你的职业生涯的想法有很大关系，就像产品经理思考他们的产品一样，策略之一是想象理想的场景，然后从那里开始逆向工作，而不是逐步前进，下一步是什么？接下来是什么？所以在这种情况下，她在想，“这就是我想要去的地方。好吧，下一步要做什么？”我喜欢那个。 (00:33:07)：本集由 Webflow 为您带来。我们都是这里的朋友，所以让我们现实一点吧。我们都知道您的网站不应该是静态资产。它应该是推动转化的策略的动态部分。那是商务 101，但这是给您的号码。 54% 的领导者表示网络更新时间太长。现在有超过一半的人在听。这就是 Webflow 的用武之地。他们的视觉优先平台允许您快速构建、启动和优化网页。这意味着您可以设定雄心勃勃的业务目标，并且您的网站可以应对挑战。立即访问 webflow.com 了解 Dropbox、IDEO 和 Orangetheory 等团队如何信任 Webflow 来实现他们最雄心勃勃的目标。 (00:33:53)：好吧，换个稍微不同的方向，我想说的是，你写的最能引起我共鸣的帖子是关于内向的人，以及作为一个内向的人要取得成功是多么困难，而基本上，作为一个内向的人，必须学会成为一个外向的人，因为在商业中，外向的人是最有价值的。您能否谈谈您的见解、您对此的看法以及您对像我这样的内向者如何在商业上取得成功以及您需要改变什么的建议？

turns.speaker: Deb Liu
turns.en: Well, first, I love the book, Quiet by Susan Cain. She talks about the power of introverts. Unfortunately, the world doesn't see the way the world the way she does. I wrote this post. It was the secret bias no one talks about, which is the workplace is really favoring people who can speak up. And I tell the story of somebody on my team who's just an amazing product manager, and yet every time she came up for promotion or calibration, people were like, "Oh, what does she do?" And it was because she was not good at broadcasting or explaining what she does. (00:34:54): I would take her to executive meetings and she was really bad at answering questions or talking. And so we would prep and prep and prep. I just knew her skills and I could see her every day moving the product forward. But for some reason people... Because your peers also have influence over people's ratings and their promotions, and I was constantly just trying to figure out how to get them to see her brilliance. I asked her once, I said, "I noticed that you never answer questions when we do these presentations." She's like, "Yeah, because I'm a processor. And by the time I process, I feel like the conversation has moved on." (00:35:28): And so I really feel like the world, it's not built for somebody like her who's a brilliant product leader, but people couldn't see it. And I realized that so much of what products and just general leadership is, is not just doing the work, but actually... It's not just having the product, it's having great product marketing to go with it. Let's call it that. Okay, so I've been in product and I've been product marketing. You make a light bulb, but you're selling light. (00:35:53): I really think about how that she was making amazing number of light bulbs. She was lighting up all the houses, but she was not marketing the light. And I think that was the thing that was really missing. Is that fair? Absolutely not. There are a lot of people who are born introverted. Is it fair that a product manager who isn't introverted, isn't extroverted is struggling with that? No, but that's the world we live in. And so it's one of those things where you get to choose what you do. (00:36:21): First, I think for the individual is realizing that you are your own best marketer. You have to actually share what you do. If a great product is out in the world, but no one is told about it, did it exist? And so one of the things that's very important is really to get that product marketing. (00:36:39): The second part is we should change our workplaces so everyone can be successful. And I think that that's a really important skill. As more introverts get into leadership, they need to actually change the world to make more space for people like them as well. So one of the things that I found was in my leadership teams over the last several years, we had this thing where we all vote, but we vote offline in a document and we put a number in and then we put our comments in. (00:37:05): And that way everyone has an equal voice in this document. And then when we talk about it, usually, of course the extroverts speak first, but everyone has a vote and we can actually see what people's point of views are. And I love that. I love that when there's something we used to do at Facebook is we used to go around in a circle and everybody would give their opinion in a meeting. I do that still today. I ask every single person as a business leader at this company, would you do this? (00:37:30): And even I joke with our chief legal officer, Greg, I say, "You are a business leader and the lawyer. You can't just say, well, legal advises X." I'm like, "But what would you do?" And so nobody can take a backseat to decision making. Everybody has a voice. So there's so many of these kind of bias interrupters, things that we can do to actually make the world easier for those who weren't speaking up and taking 80% of the air in the room. And I do think that we have to craft a workplace where everyone can be their best.
turns.zh: 嗯，首先，我喜欢苏珊·凯恩的《安静》这本书。她谈论内向者的力量。不幸的是，世界并不像她那样看待世界。我写了这篇文章。这是一种没有人谈论的秘密偏见，即职场确实偏爱敢于发声的人。我讲述了我团队中某人的故事，她是一位出色的产品经理，但每次她提出晋升或校准时，人们都会说，“哦，她是做什么的？”这是因为她不擅长传播或解释自己所做的事情。 (00:34:54)：我会带她参加高管会议，但她真的不擅长回答问题或说话。所以我们会准备、准备、准备。我只是了解她的技能，我可以看到她每天都在推动产品向前发展。但出于某种原因，人们……因为你的同龄人也会影响人们的收视率和晋升，而我一直在想办法让他们看到她的才华。有一次我问她，我说：“我注意到我们做这些演示时你从不回答问题。”她说，“是的，因为我是一个处理者。当我处理时，我觉得谈话已经继续了。” (00:35:28)：所以我真的觉得这个世界不是为像她这样出色的产品领导者而建的，但人们看不到它。我意识到产品和一般领导力的大部分内容不仅仅是做工作，而且实际上......它不仅仅是拥有产品，还拥有与之相伴的出色的产品营销。我们就这么称呼它吧。好的，我一直从事产品和产品营销工作。你制造一个灯泡，但你却在卖灯。 (00:35:53)：我真的很想她是如何制作出数量惊人的灯泡的。她照亮了所有的房子，但她并没有推销这种光。我认为这才是真正缺失的东西。这公平吗？绝对不是。有很多人天生内向。一个不内向、不外向的产品经理正在为此苦苦挣扎，这公平吗？不，但这就是我们生活的世界。所以这是你可以选择做什么的事情之一。 (00:36:21)：首先，我认为对于个人来说，要意识到你自己就是最好的营销人员。你必须实际分享你所做的事情。如果世界上出现了一种伟大的产品，但没有人知道它，那么它存在吗？因此，非常重要的事情之一就是进行产品营销。 (00:36:39)：第二部分是我们应该改变我们的工作场所，以便每个人都能成功。我认为这是一项非常重要的技能。随着越来越多的内向者进入领导层，他们需要真正改变世界，为像他们这样的人腾出更多空间。所以我发现的一件事是在过去几年里我的领导团队中，我们有这样的事情，我们所有人都投票，但我们在文件中离线投票，我们输入一个数字，然后我们输入我们的评论。（00:37:05）：这样每个人在这份文件中都有平等的发言权。当我们谈论这个问题时，通常，当然是外向的人先发言，但每个人都有投票权，我们实际上可以看到人们的观点是什么。我喜欢这样。我喜欢我们过去在 Facebook 做的事情，就是我们围成一圈，每个人都会在会议上发表自己的意见。我今天仍然这样做。我问每个公司的业务领导者，你会这样做吗？ (00:37:30)：即使我和我们的首席法律官格雷格开玩笑，我也会说，“你是商业领袖和律师。你不能只是说，嗯，法律建议 X。”我想，“但是你会怎么做？”因此，没有人可以在决策过程中退居二线。每个人都有发言权。因此，有很多这样的偏见干扰者，我们可以做一些事情，让那些没有发言、占据房间里 80% 空气的人的生活变得更轻松。我确实认为我们必须打造一个让每个人都能做到最好的工作场所。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: In the post, you also talk about as much as we want to change the way people run their companies and think. I love your advice of you also still have to learn how to speak up and act more extroverted even though it's not natural to you. Is that right?
turns.zh: 在这篇文章中，您还谈到了我们希望改变人们经营公司和思维方式的内容。我喜欢你的建议，你仍然需要学习如何说话和表现得更外向，尽管这对你来说并不自然。是这样吗？

turns.speaker: Deb Liu
turns.en: I think we do a disservice when we say we're not good at speaking up because it's a skill like any other. And if I told you the difference between your product being successful and not being successful is you giving this presentation, they're going to kill your product if you don't sell this to the executives. You would figure out a way to stand in front of those executives and defend the freaking heck out of your product. But why aren't you doing that every day? (00:38:35): And I think sometimes we forget that not everything is as essential as they're going to cut your product if you can't convince them to keep it. But every day you're actually building credibility for your team, getting more resources, getting more people to talk about your product inside your company, getting more press for the product outside. All of those things combined into momentum for your product. And don't you want the best thing for your product and your customers? (00:38:58): So if you think about it that way, it's not, well, I'm uncomfortable. I hear this a lot where people say, "Well, you wouldn't understand. I'm an introvert." And I'm like, "So was I." But instead I just said, "Okay, this is a necessary skill and it's a learnable skill. You don't have to be comfortable with it. You don't have to love it, but you just have to do it."
turns.zh: 我认为，当我们说自己不擅长发声时，我们就造成了伤害，因为这是一种与其他技能一样的技能。如果我告诉你你的产品成功与不成功之间的区别就在于你是否进行了这次演示，那么如果你不将其出售给高管，他们就会杀死你的产品。你会想办法站在那些高管面前，为你的产品辩护。但你为什么不每天都这样做呢？ (00:38:35)：我认为有时我们会忘记，并不是所有事情都那么重要，因为如果你不能说服他们保留你的产品，他们就会削减你的产品。但每天你实际上都在为你的团队建立信誉，获得更多资源，让更多的人在公司内部谈论你的产品，在外部获得更多关于产品的媒体报道。所有这些因素结合起来为您的产品带来动力。您难道不想为您的产品和客户提供最好的东西吗？ (00:38:58)：所以如果你这样想的话，我就不会感到不舒服。我经常听到人们说：“好吧，你不会理解的。我是一个内向的人。”我想，“我也是。”但我只是说：“好吧，这是一项必要的技能，而且是一项可以学习的技能。你不必对它感到舒服。你不必喜欢它，但你只需要做它。”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What about from another perspective of why people don't do this, which is it feels like self-promotion and it feels like icky like, "I'm just sitting around promoting myself. I don't want to be doing that." Anything there that helps people get over that piece?
turns.zh: 从另一个角度来看人们为什么不这样做，这感觉像是自我推销，而且感觉很恶心，“我只是坐着推销自己。我不想这样做。”有什么可以帮助人们克服这个问题吗？

turns.speaker: Deb Liu
turns.en: Well, I just remember I was talking to this ERG group and I was asking about... There was an upcoming calibration and self reviews were due in a couple of days. And I said, "Well, what are you doing for your self-review?" And somebody raised their hand and said, "Well, I'm really bad at self-promotion. What advice would you have for me?" And I said, "If you think your self-review is self-promotion, you're just not going to do a great job at it." (00:39:56): What if I called it educating your manager about all the great work your team has been doing? What if I called it helping people see why your team should get more resources? Suddenly you're cracking open, you're changing the question right from, "Oh, I was self-promoting to actually I'm helping my team get more resources and support." And suddenly she was like, "Oh yeah, I never thought about it that way." (00:40:22): But I think often if you frame it one way, it looks like self-promotion. I wouldn't want to do that because of self-promotion. But at the same time, if it's education, what if I said, "I was talking to a PM who's really incredible. I've mentored him and sponsored him for a long time." And I said, "I don't understand why you don't have more of a voice. You've learned so much about the craft. You've done this at multiple companies." And he said exactly what you said which is I'm not really self-promoting. (00:40:46): And I said, "If you see it as self-promoting, you will never do it." And so let's talk about why you don't actually do this. And he said, "I've seen a lot of people who are really great on LinkedIn write these articles, but they have nothing to back it up." And I don't want to be like them. And I said, "Okay. Well, you read my blog, you follow me on LinkedIn, do you think I have nothing to black back it up?" And he's like, "No, of course not." (00:41:07): And I said, "Well, then why do you put yourself in his category instead of mine?" And I think it was just a moment where we just came to an understanding where he in his mind was like, "I don't want to be that person. It's an empty vessel that has no substance behind it." And I said, "Do you think the things I write have no substance?" But it was an interesting conversation because he had taken this mantle that it was self-promotion and that behind what if people think I'm nothing behind it?" (00:41:32): I'm like, "I know you have something behind this. I have been your manager. I have worked with you for many years, but you see how just reframing it has really changed his way of thinking about it." Still working on him. But I actually think he has so much to give and I think he has learned so much about the craft, and I wish that more product managers feel comfortable that they have something to give to the world.
turns.zh: 好吧，我只记得我正在与这个 ERG 小组交谈，我问的是……即将进行校准，自我审查将在几天内完成。我说：“那么，你在做什么自我审查呢？”有人举手说：“好吧，我真的不擅长自我推销。你对我有什么建议吗？”我说：“如果你认为自我审查是自我推销，那么你就不会做得很好。” (00:39:56)：如果我称其为向您的经理介绍您的团队所做的所有出色工作呢？如果我称其为帮助人们了解为什么您的团队应该获得更多资源呢？突然间，你敞开心扉，将问题从“哦，我是在自我推销，实际上我是在帮助我的团队获得更多资源和支持。”突然她说：“哦，是的，我从来没有那样想过。” (00:40:22)：但我认为，如果以一种方式来表述，通常看起来就像是自我推销。我不想因为自我推销而这样做。但与此同时，如果是教育，如果我说：“我正在和一位非常令人难以置信的总理交谈。我长期以来一直指导并赞助他。”我说：“我不明白为什么你没有更多的发言权。你在这门手艺上学到了很多东西。你在多家公司都做过这件事。”他说的正是你所说的，我并不是在自我推销。 (00:40:46)：我说，“如果你认为这是自我推销，你就永远不会这么做。”那么让我们来谈谈为什么你不真正这样做。他说：“我在 LinkedIn 上看到很多非常优秀的人写了这些文章，但他们没有任何支持。”我不想像他们一样。我说：“好吧。好吧，你读了我的博客，在 LinkedIn 上关注了我，你认为我没有什么可以黑的吗？”他说：“不，当然不是。” (00:41:07)：我说：“那你为什么把自己归入他的类别而不是我的类别呢？”我认为那只是一个时刻，我们才了解到他内心的想法，“我不想成为那个人。它是一个空容器，背后没有任何实质内容。”我说：“你觉得我写的东西没有实质内容吗？”但这是一次有趣的谈话，因为他认为这是自我推销，如果人们认为我什么都没有背后怎么办？”（00:41:32）：我想，“我知道你背后有一些东西。我曾经是你的经理。我和你一起工作了很多年，但你会发现，仅仅重新构建它就真的改变了他的思考方式。”仍在为他工作。但实际上我认为他有很多东西可以奉献，我认为他在这门手艺上学到了很多东西，我希望更多的产品经理感到放心，因为他们可以向世界奉献一些东西。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I think what you're saying right now will resonate with a lot of people when they see people posting. I feel the still of just like, "I don't want to be this guy that's just posting nonsense on LinkedIn just to get likes," even though it's kind of what I do now full time. Hopefully it's not nonsense.
turns.zh: 我认为当很多人看到人们发帖时，你现在所说的会引起共鸣。我仍然觉得，“我不想成为这个在 LinkedIn 上发布废话只是为了博取赞的人”，尽管这就是我现在全职做的事情。希望这不是废话。

turns.speaker: Deb Liu
turns.en: But it is all substance. So, Lenny, we know the substance behind it.
turns.zh: 但这都是物质。所以，莱尼，我们知道其背后的实质。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I tried, but I think there's posting on LinkedIn, posting on Twitter. There's like an innate just doing this because I want to get attention when often... And the way I started this is just like things I've learned that I think are useful, I'm just going to put them out there. So just to double click a little bit, I think this is a really powerful point. What actually have you found helps people get over that? Is it someone like you and his corner being like, "You have really great stuff to share, you should actually do it. Don't be as worried as you are, as you think you might be." Is there anything else that works there?
turns.zh: 我试过了，但我认为 LinkedIn 上有发帖，Twitter 上有发帖。就像我天生就这样做，因为我想经常引起注意……我开始这样做的方式就像我学到的我认为有用的东西一样，我只是要把它们放在那里。所以只要双击一下，​​我认为这是一个非常强大的点。您实际上发现了什么可以帮助人们克服这个问题？是不是像你这样的人和他的角落一样，“你有很棒的东西要分享，你实际上应该这样做。不要像你想象的那样担心。”还有其他东西可以在那里工作吗？

turns.speaker: Deb Liu
turns.en: Actually what worked for me was I was working with Bos and I talk about our relationship in my book, but we made a contract when I started reporting to him. And Bos, for those of you don't know, is currently the CTO of Meta. At the time he was the head of ads and then our team moved into his team. And so I was reorged into his organization. And as I said we did not have the best relationship before that. And so we made a contract to work together and I had written like, "Here's how I want you to take care of my team. Here's how I want you to support our products." And I wrote them this long, my part of the commitment. (00:43:13): Then he wrote back, "Here's what I'm asking of you. I want you to write and publish something every month." I was like, "What are you talking about? Why would you say that?" He said, "You have so much to teach people. Just do it." I said, "I don't really have that much to say." And he's like, "Just trust me on this. You'll figure it out." His advice was write what you repeat. If you say something more than once, just write it down. And then the next time someone asks you, you can just hand them. (00:43:40): He has a great blog if you have read it. I just normally thinking that is a weird thing for your new manager to say after you had a lot of conflict together before that. But he took my contract, which was... By the way, he's like, "Oh, do you want to codify this in some way?" I'm like, "No, I just..." But every month from then on, I would literally just write something and it was my promise to him. And I did it faithfully and I published it internally. So I didn't publish it externally for a long time. (00:44:04): And then sometimes they would ask me if I want to publish it externally for the company and I would say yes. And so I did it for years. I reported to him for years. And then we switched managers. He moved over to Reality Labs and then I had a new manager and I continued and I continued this. Then I started doing a publicly, and then obviously I wrote a book. Because of him and his encouragement, it got me to a totally different place. And part of it was just the commitment. I now had accountability because I knew he was watching. I'm not actually sure if he was actually watching every month. But I felt the accountability to do this and I've done it every single month since.
turns.zh: 事实上，对我有用的是我和博斯一起工作，我在书中谈论了我们的关系，但当我开始向他汇报时，我们签订了合同。对于那些不知道的人来说，Bos 目前是 Meta 的 CTO。当时他是广告主管，然后我们的团队就搬到了他的团队。于是我就被重组到了他的组织中。正如我所说，在那之前我们的关系并不是最好的。所以我们签订了一份合作合同，我写道：“这就是我希望你如何照顾我的团队。这就是我希望你如何支持我们的产品。”我写了这么长的内容，这是我的承诺的一部分。 (00:43:13)：然后他回信说：“这就是我对你的要求。我希望你每个月都写一些东西并发表一些东西。”我当时想，“你在说什么？你为什么这么说？”他说：“你有很多东西可以教给人们。就去做吧。”我说：“我其实没什么可说的。”他说：“相信我。你会解决的。”他的建议是写下你重复的内容。如果某件事你说了不止一次，就把它写下来。然后下次有人问你时，你就可以递给他们。 (00:43:40)：如果你读过的话，他有一个很棒的博客。我通常认为，在你们之前发生过很多冲突之后，你的新经理说出这样的话是很奇怪的。但他拿走了我的合同，这是......顺便说一句，他就像，“哦，你想以某种方式将其编入法典吗？”我想，“不，我只是……”但从那以后的每个月，我都会写一些东西，这是我对他的承诺。我忠实地做到了这一点，并在内部发布了它。所以我很长一段时间都没有对外发布。 (00:44:04)：有时他们会问我是否想为公司向外部发布它，我会说是。我就这样做了很多年。我向他汇报了很多年。然后我们更换了经理。他转到现实实验室，然后我有了一位新经理，我继续这样做。然后我开始公开做，然后显然我写了一本书。因为他和他的鼓励，我到达了一个完全不同的地方。其中一部分只是承诺。我现在有责任因为我知道他在看着。我实际上不确定他是否真的每个月都在看。但我感到有责任这样做，从那以后我每个月都这样做。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So it's interesting that that's another example of your manager giving you the space slash forcing you to share publicly being a really good lever to get someone over this fear.
turns.zh: 因此，有趣的是，这是你的经理给你空格斜杠的另一个例子，迫使你公开分享，这是让某人克服这种恐惧的一个非常好的杠杆。

turns.speaker: Deb Liu
turns.en: I think sometimes just doing it gets you over the hump. For example, my friend, Ami Vora. She writes an incredible blog. You have not read her Substack, you should. But she's an incredible writer. She'd write all these things internally and I said, "You should publish this externally." Now she does that and it's really great. And I think part of it was just seeing her just put it out there because she is one of the wisest career coaches that I have and managers that I have ever worked with. And so I'm like, "You have so much to say and to share." (00:45:16): So to see it out there, I feel like for years we all got the benefit of it because we knew her. But the world was not getting the benefit. So in some ways just having accountability. So we created a little accountability group to help each other write, and it was just a reminder, "Hey, did you do it?" And so I think it's sometimes what's necessary to get over that hump is either having someone forcing you, like your manager who you made a commitment to, or just having a friend to say, "Hey, by the way, where's this month's post?" (00:45:41): Those things matter because now you got over the hump of, "I have to do it." And now it's just about how good you're going to make it and how much time you're going to put into it.
turns.zh: 我认为有时只要这样做就能让你渡过难关。例如，我的朋友阿米·沃拉。她写了一个令人难以置信的博客。你还没有读过她的 Substack，你应该读。但她是一位令人难以置信的作家。她会在内部写下所有这些内容，我说：“你应该在外部发布这些内容。”现在她做到了，这真的很棒。我认为部分原因只是看到她把它放在那里，因为她是我所拥有的最明智的职业教练和我共事过的经理之一。所以我想，“你有很多话要说和分享。” (00:45:16)：所以看到它在那里，我觉得多年来我们都从中受益，因为我们认识她。但世界并没有从中受益。所以在某些方面只是有责任。因此，我们创建了一个小型问责小组来帮助彼此写作，这只是一个提醒，“嘿，你做到了吗？”所以我认为有时要克服这个困难，要么有人强迫你，比如你向你做出承诺的经理，要么只是有一个朋友说，“嘿，顺便问一下，这个月的帖子在哪里？” (00:45:41)：这些事情很重要，因为现在你已经克服了“我必须这样做”的困难。现在关键在于你要做得有多好以及你要投入多少时间。

turns.speaker: Deb Liu

turns.en: Yeah, she's amazing. She has a great Substack. We'll link to it again in the show notes. We'll link to your Substack as well.
