turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Go Substack. I want to move in a slightly different direction. Talk about growth for a little bit. You have a really nice perspective on how to think about growth. I think a lot of people think of growth as like, "Here's a magic bullet. We're going to do this thing. It's going to go, "Wow, we're going to win." And your approach is, you talk about it, it's a game of inches. Growth is a game of inches. Can you talk about your perspective there?
turns.zh: 转到子堆栈。我想朝稍微不同的方向前进。稍微谈谈成长。您对如何思考增长有非常好的看法。我认为很多人认为增长就像是，“这是一个神奇的子弹。我们要做这件事。它会说，“哇，我们会赢。”你的方法是，你谈论它，这是一场英寸游戏。增长是一场英寸游戏。你能谈谈你的观点吗？

turns.speaker: Deb Liu
turns.en: Yeah. Sometimes we think it's like what is the huge step function? But actually most companies are like... We call it points of growth, right? It's like if you can move things 1% a little bit faster every single week, think about the amount of growth you get at the end. And so it's not just, "Okay, what's going to get you the 3X? You can get to 3X 1% at a time, 5% at a time. Single digit growth. And sometimes it is the small things that matter the most. And so we think about product-led growth, it's really about finding the aha moments, the opportunities. And sometimes opportunities are things that seem really silly. (00:47:10): I heard the story at Facebook that one of the big things was just adding the, next to ads, they put the word create an ad, was one of the biggest growth drivers. And that was it just putting a link because people just didn't know how to get to the ads flow. It was things like that where you can actually bend the curve of choices that you make. Same thing, each of the growth teams I've ever worked on, it's like really the small things adding up. It is a list we used to work on payments growth and we had a list of a hundred things we were working on hypotheses. (00:47:42): And then we would pick and we would grow them by picking the first 10 and we would start working on them, the next 10, the next 10, and we would go through these sprint cycles. And the same thing when we were growing the ads product as well. Marketplace, each of them were just like, "What are the small things that add up to big things?" And I think sometimes we overthink it. (00:48:00): Instead, you probably have a hundred ideas. And by the way, it is absolutely okay if the 80% of them don't work. I tell people sometimes we overthink as product manager if we just had the perfect plan, the perfect battle plan, but instead imagine you're a team and you can ship, I don't know, let's say four things. But what if you're a team that can ship 20 things with the same with a 20% success. You get just as much output and yet you know what doesn't work also. (00:48:30): What if you can move it from 20% to 30%? Suddenly six things work, not just four things. And so in the same amount of time you have all the lessons of what didn't work, plus you're getting 50% more output. And so you thinking about growth as this engine of, it's a learning machine of what doesn't work, what you reiterate on, what you change, and you're constantly getting better and better and better.
turns.zh: 是的。有时我们会想这就像巨大的阶跃函数是什么？但实际上大多数公司就像......我们称之为增长点，对吧？这就像如果你可以每周把事情加快 1% 一点，想想你最终获得的增长量。所以这不仅仅是，“好吧，什么能让你获得 3 倍？你一次可以达到 3 倍 1%，一次 5%。单位数增长。有时最重要的是小事情。所以我们考虑产品主导的增长，这实际上是寻找顿悟时刻和机会。有时机会是看起来非常愚蠢的事情。(00:47:10)：我在 Facebook 听到了一个故事，其中一个最大的事情就是在广告旁边添加“创建广告”这个词，这是最大的增长动力之一，因为人们不知道如何进入广告流程，就像这样，你可以真正改变你所做的选择曲线。 (00:47:42)：然后我们会选择并通过选择前 10 个来发展它们，然后开始研究接下来的 10 个、接下来的 10 个，当我们开发广告产品时，我们也会经历同样的事情，每个都是这样的，“什么是小事情，加起来就是大事情？” (00:48:00)：相反，你可能有一百个想法。顺便说一句，如果我告诉人们，作为产品经理，我们有时会过度思考，如果我们有完美的计划，完美的战斗计划，但相反，想象你是一个团队，你可以交付，我不知道，让我们说四件事，但如果你是一个团队，可以交付 20 件相同的事情，但成功率只有 20%。 (00:48:30)：如果你能把它从 20% 提高到 30%，结果会怎样？突然间，有 6 件事情有效，而不仅仅是 4 件事情。因此，在相同的时间内，你获得了所有无效的教训，而且你还获得了 50% 的额外产出，所以你将增长视为一个学习机器，学习什么是无效的，什么是你重申的，什么是你的。改变，你就会不断变得越来越好。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I think what you're saying will resonate with a lot of product people where there's always this like, "We're just doing a bunch of optimization, incremental work. Still sucks, boring. Let's take some big bets." And in my experience, and sounds like in your experience, a lot of the wins actually... And Facebook is famous for this, just relentlessly looking for ways to grow, optimize, optimize, optimize because that's where a lot of growth comes from. (00:49:14): At the same time, obviously you need to take some big bets and take some swings and look for step function changes. But I guess for someone that's just like... I don't know. Is there any advice on just creating that culture of like, "It's okay to optimize for a long time, there's a lot of opportunity optimizing"? Is there anything you've learned there or is it just bringing in a Deb and it has to be a top down?
turns.zh: 我认为你所说的会引起很多产品人员的共鸣，他们总是这样说，“我们只是在做一堆优化、增量工作。仍然很糟糕、无聊。让我们赌一些大赌注。”根据我的经验，听起来也像你的经验一样，实际上有很多胜利……Facebook 以此而闻名，只是不懈地寻找增长、优化、优化、优化的方法，因为这就是很多增长的来源。 (00:49:14)：同时，显然你需要下一些大赌注，进行一些调整，寻找阶跃函数的变化。但我想对于那些就像……我不知道的人。对于创建“长时间优化没关系，有很多优化机会”这样的文化有什么建议吗？你在那里学到了什么，还是只是引入了 Deb 并且必须是自上而下的？

turns.speaker: Deb Liu
turns.en: I treat growth like, let's say, a product marketing team. It is an augmentation for a product that works. So if you have a core product that works, you have a team that's working on... So for us at Ancestry, it's like search and hints of the core. What is the mechanics? You want people to add people to their family tree. You want them to add stories, okay? There's teams that make sure that the uptime is good, that the hints are working, the search delivers results. (00:49:57): And you need those teams, you need those core teams kind of functioning. But growth is actually optimization on top. It is making it so that you get to the search flow faster. The hints are surfacing better, that people are accepting them, that if we put the button here versus here, that people are going to discover things faster. And so it's really taking the core engine and actually wrapping it around the user interface around the experience, around the flows so that people can get to it faster, they can have more satisfaction, they can have more impact. And that's what I see growth as. It's not the core product. It is the cherry on top, making that product more accessible and more usable and better every single day.
turns.zh: 我将成长视为产品营销团队。它是对有效产品的增强。因此，如果你有一个有效的核心产品，你就有一个团队正在努力……所以对于我们 Ancestry 来说，这就像核心的搜索和提示。其机理是什么？您希望人们将人员添加到他们的家谱中。你想让他们添加故事，好吗？有些团队会确保正常运行时间良好、提示有效、搜索提供结果。 (00:49:57)：你需要这些团队，你需要那些核心团队的运作。但增长实际上是最重要的优化。它使您能够更快地进入搜索流程。提示浮现得更好，人们正在接受它们，如果我们把按钮放在这里而不是放在这里，人们会更快地发现事物。因此，它实际上采用了核心引擎，并将其围绕体验、流程围绕用户界面进行包装，以便人们可以更快地使用它，他们可以获得更多满足感，他们可以产生更大影响。这就是我所看到的增长。这不是核心产品。它是最重要的，使该产品变得更容易获得、更可用、每天都变得更好。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Along these lines, I think it surprised people to learn. There's at least a hundred people at our Airbnb just working on pricing, optimizing pricing recommendations. There's endless opportunity to just make all these core components of an experience better and better and better over time. Okay. Last thing I want to talk about, and this is completely unrelated to everything we've been talking about mostly, which is your 30, 60, 90-day plan. (00:51:00): So you wrote this post a while ago, just like, here's a great 30, 60, 90-day plan when you join a company. I've heard that many people use this. It's really effective for helping someone onboard and be successful. And I think it's mostly for execs or is this for just anyone joining a company?
turns.zh: 沿着这些思路，我认为人们的学习感到惊讶。我们的 Airbnb 至少有 100 名员工负责定价、优化定价建议。随着时间的推移，有无限的机会让体验的所有这些核心组成部分变得越来越好。好的。我想谈的最后一件事，这与我们主要谈论的所有事情完全无关，即你的 30、60、90 天计划。 (00:51:00)：所以你不久前写了这篇文章，就像，当你加入一家公司时，这里有一个很棒的 30 天、60 天、90 天计划。我听说很多人都用这个。它对于帮助某人加入并取得成功确实非常有效。我认为这主要是针对高管的，还是只针对任何加入公司的人？

turns.speaker: Deb Liu
turns.en: It's for anyone.
turns.zh: 它适合任何人。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, anyone.
turns.zh: 好吧，任何人。

turns.speaker: Deb Liu
turns.en: I created, it's actually when I joined Ancestry because I hadn't started a real new job in 11 years. And I thought, I'm going to be a student of how to land well. So I read a bunch of things, I read and I decided I was going to adapt all of those things into a summary and then I was going to try it real time in my blog. (00:51:38): So in my blog I write, "Here's what I'm going to do," and then I tell you what I did and how it worked and some things. And then I actually do a look back as to all the mistakes I made. And so I did this live. It was not planned quite as well as I would thought, but I put it together and I wrote the 30, 60, 90-day plan and I have a template. I always tell people it's focused on listening and learning first and then doing. So that's the crux of it, which is in those 90-days it's like you got to get used to the environment. You want to have some impact at the start. You want to have a couple quick wins, but you want to understand the lay of the land and you want to listen because you have something to contribute. (00:52:19): But if you don't understand the language, you don't understand the culture, you might actually make huge mistakes. And so for the first 30 days, I did a listening tour. I talked to over 60 people in 30 days and then I summarized a state of the union. Here's what I'm hearing, here are the challenges people feel like we're facing. Here's what people's wishlists are. And by the way, one person sent me a wishlist of five things and at that year, I think it took me till year two to finish his five things. And then I sent him a note. I said, "By the way, the first time we met, these five things you wanted to see, we just finished the last one." (00:52:50): And he's like, "I can't believe you remember." I took extensive notes and I summarized it. I think it's important because people want to hear that you hear them. And you don't have to be a manager or CEO to do that. I think people on teams often feel like there's no outlet for the things that they want to say. I encourage, especially product leaders, especially if you're joining an existing team, to listen really behind what people are saying and then offer to help them do one thing. (00:53:17): So especially when you're meeting with a new engineering team for the first time, actually ask them, what is one thing I can do to help you this week? I always say one thing, it's limited. This week, so getting 15 new headcount. Probably not going to happen. And it's like, how can I give back? And suddenly you're building a reciprocal relationship. And so a lot of this 30, 60, 90-day plan is really to help you find your footing and then to start having impact immediately.
turns.zh: 我创建的，实际上是在我加入 Ancestry 的时候，因为我已经 11 年没有开始真正的新工作了。我想，我要成为一名如何良好着陆的学生。所以我读了很多东西，我读了，我决定将所有这些东西改编成一个摘要，然后我将在我的博客中实时尝试。 (00:51:38)：所以在我的博客中我写道，“这就是我要做的事情”，然后我告诉你我做了什么、它是如何运作的以及一些事情。然后我实际上回顾了我所犯的所有错误。所以我现场做了这个。它的计划并不像我想象的那么好，但我把它放在一起，写了 30 天、60 天、90 天的计划，我有一个模板。我总是告诉人们首先要注重倾听和学习，然后再去做。所以这就是问题的关键，那就是在这90天里你必须适应环境。您希望在一开始就产生一些影响。你想要快速取得一些胜利，但你想要了解情况并且想要倾听，因为你可以做出一些贡献。 (00:52:19)：但是如果你不了解语言，不了解文化，你实际上可能会犯下巨大的错误。因此，在前 30 天里，我进行了一次聆听之旅。我在 30 天内与 60 多人交谈，然后总结了国情咨文。这是我所听到的，这是人们认为我们面临的挑战。这是人们的愿望清单。顺便说一句，有一个人给我发了一份包含五件事的愿望清单，那一年，我想我花了第二年才完成他的五件事。然后我给他发了一张纸条。我说：“对了，我们第一次见面，你想看的这五件事，我们刚刚完成了最后一个。” (00:52:50)：他说，“我不敢相信你还记得。”我做了很多笔记并总结了它。我认为这很重要，因为人们希望听到你听到他们的声音。而且您不必成为经理或首席执行官才能做到这一点。我认为团队中的人们常常觉得他们想说的话没有出口。我鼓励，特别是产品领导者，特别是如果你要加入现有的团队，要真正倾听人们的意见，然后主动帮助他们做一件事。 (00:53:17)：因此，尤其是当您第一次与新的工程团队会面时，请实际询问他们，本周我可以做些什么来帮助您？我总是说一件事，它是有限的。本周，新增 15 名员工。可能不会发生。就像，我该如何回报？突然之间，你们就建立了一种互惠的关系。因此，这个 30 天、60 天、90 天计划的大部分内容实际上是为了帮助您找到立足点，然后立即开始产生影响。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Say you join a company and you're like, "I'm going to do 30 days listening," and then your boss is like, "No, we need to ship stuff. Get on it, ship this stuff." Is there any advice for trying to push back on that, create space for listening when there's deadlines, things aren't [inaudible 00:53:56]?
turns.zh: 假设你加入一家公司，你会说，“我要听 30 天”，然后你的老板会说，“不，我们需要运送东西。开始吧，运送这些东西。”有没有什么建议可以尝试推迟这一点，在截止日期到来时创造聆听空间，事情没有[听不清00:53:56]？

turns.speaker: Deb Liu
turns.en: I encourage everybody to get on the same page on this 30, 60, 90-day plan with their manager. So actually don't just keep it to yourself. Share it with as many people as you can. So I think it's very important that everyone sees what you're trying to accomplish and what your output is going to be. Because if you don't know the output, is success there? The second part is with your manager say, "Okay. I would like to carve 20% of my time listening and I'm happy to do this work 80% of the time." Therefore every morning from nine to 10, I want to talk to somebody in the organization. (00:54:28): Just make sure you say, "I will do a better job and have more impact if I have this time to make sure that I'm not accidentally making mistake or I don't get a chance, I'm asking something of somebody, but I've never met them." And to really carve out space because it's really important. Once you're in it, people give you the new person card for maybe a month or two and then suddenly it's all the problems are your problems. (00:54:53): But what if you don't know what the problems are? And so I always say diagnose before you treat. So make sure you understand so that you can help and deliver what your manager is actually expecting of you.
turns.zh: 我鼓励每个人与他们的经理就这个 30 天、60 天、90 天计划达成一致。所以实际上不要只把它留给自己。与尽可能多的人分享。所以我认为让每个人都看到你想要完成什么以及你的产出是什么是非常重要的。因为如果你不知道输出，那成功了吗？第二部分是对你的经理说：“好吧。我愿意花 20% 的时间来倾听，而且我很乐意用 80% 的时间来做这项工作。”因此每天早上九点到十点，我想和组织里的某个人谈谈。 (00:54:28)：只要确保你说：“如果我有这个时间来确保我不会无意中犯错误或我没有机会，我会做得更好并产生更大的影响，我正在向某人询问一些事情，但我从未见过他们。”并真正开辟空间，因为这非常重要。一旦你加入其中，人们会给你新的人员卡，也许一两个月，然后突然间，所有的问题都是你的问题。 (00:54:53)：但是如果您不知道问题是什么怎么办？所以我总是说先诊断再治疗。因此，请确保您理解，以便您可以帮助并实现经理对您的实际期望。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I'm looking at your template. So just to share the bucket. So first 30 days learning focus, second 30 days is aligning on vision for the future, and the last 30 days of the 90 days is executing, setting up, actually starting to get stuff done. Awesome. Anything else along these lines of this?
turns.zh: 我正在看你的模板。所以只是分享桶。因此，前 30 天是学习重点，第二个 30 天是调整未来的愿景，而 90 天的最后 30 天是执行、设置、实际开始完成工作。惊人的。与此相关的还有其他内容吗？

turns.speaker: Deb Liu
turns.en: The one thing about having a plan also is that you don't feel rushed to do something that you're not ready for because I do think sometimes you feel like you need to have impact. I always tell people, "Do something small, give back in some ways that people see you making." But when you actually reflect, one of the biggest things I could do was actually reflect back to the organization, "Here's what I heard from all of you. I'm listening, I hear this and here's what I want to do about it." (00:55:53): And then in aligning it's like, "Do we agree this is a set of problems we want to tackle?" And then an execution is like, "Do we agree that this is how we want to move forward?" And I think that is such an important part of building into a team. When you enter an organization, you're also entering a team and you're part of a dance that's going around. What role do you play? And people are dancing around you and if you actually make a mistake, you could trip other people up as well. So really finding your place in the dance is really important.
turns.zh: 制定计划的另一件事是，你不会感到匆忙去做一些你还没有准备好的事情，因为我确实认为有时你觉得你需要产生影响。我总是告诉人们，“做一些小事，以人们看到你所做的一些方式回馈社会。”但当你真正反思时，我能做的最重要的事情之一实际上就是向组织反映，“这是我从你们所有人那里听到的。我正在倾听，我听到了这个，这就是我想做的事情。” (00:55:53)：然后在调整时就像是，“我们是否同意这是我们想要解决的一系列问题？”然后执行就像，“我们同意这就是我们想要前进的方式吗？”我认为这是构建团队的重要组成部分。当你进入一个组织时，你也就进入了一个团队，并且你成为了舞蹈的一部分。你扮演什么角色？人们在你周围跳舞，如果你真的犯了错误，你也可能会绊倒其他人。因此，真正找到自己在舞蹈中的位置非常重要。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And as a PM, the way I always think about is people won't assume they should trust you. You're just this person that's coming in to tell them what to do and so much of your first month, two, three is building that trust with people so that they can actually feel comfortable listening to your guidance and not just like, "Oh my god. This person is getting in my way."
turns.zh: 作为一名产品经理，我一直认为人们不会认为他们应该信任你。你只是一个来告诉他们该做什么的人，你的第一个月、第二个月、第三个月的大部分时间都是在与人们建立信任，这样他们就能真正放心地倾听你的指导，而不仅仅是说，“天哪。这个人妨碍了我。”

turns.speaker: Deb Liu
turns.en: And earning that trust, sometimes people really... You'd be really surprised, a lot of people feel like they're not heard and even just coming in and listening is a trust building exercise.
turns.zh: 赢得这种信任，有时人们真的......你会感到非常惊讶，很多人觉得他们没有被听到，甚至只是进来倾听也是一种建立信任的练习。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Such a good point. As we wrap up our conversation, just a couple more questions here. So first is I want to take us to Contrarian Corner, which is a segment on this podcast. And my question is there something that you believe that you think most other people don't believe? Something that you think is a contrarian perspective?
turns.zh: 这是一个很好的观点。当我们结束谈话时，还有几个问题。首先，我想带我们去“逆向角落”，这是该播客的一个部分。我的问题是，有一些你认为大多数人不相信的事情吗？您认为什么是逆向观点？

turns.speaker: Deb Liu
turns.en: I don't know if this is a contrarian perspective, but I go to speak in a lot of universities. So I speak at Stanford and I'm going to speak at Duke. And I always tell people, especially young people, the most important career decision you make is who you marry. And it's not something we think that much about, especially I started dating... I met my husband when I was 18, my first weekend in college. Started dating when I was 19. We had no idea what our life was going to be like and yet every single day like this week we had our board meeting, I was in Utah the whole week. I come home and he's taking care of everything. (00:57:43): You will have a much more successful career if your home life is in balance. It's like a yin and a yang. If something is out of balance, it engulfs the other side. Both your job and your home life. And especially, we have three kids. Really balancing that is very hard over both of us having demanding careers. It's not something that's contrarian, but it's something which we don't think about at all when we make that decision. We think is this person fun to be with? Is this person somebody we see ourselves with? But my question is what is the impact of this relationship on your career? (00:58:14): Is this person lifting you up or pushing you back? Is this person someone who's going to be your greatest cheerleader or are they going to be the greatest weight on you? How do you think that that's going to manifest itself 20 years, 30 years from now? And I think it's just something I wish we thought about more and I encourage especially young people to think about that.
turns.zh: 我不知道这是否是逆向观点，但我去很多大学演讲。我将在斯坦福大学演讲，并将在杜克大学演讲。我总是告诉人们，尤其是年轻人，你做出的最重要的职业决定就是你嫁给谁。这不是我们想得太多的事情，尤其是我开始约会……我18岁那年认识了我的丈夫，那是我上大学的第一个周末。我 19 岁开始约会。我们不知道我们的生活会是什么样子，但像本周这样的每一天我们都会召开董事会会议，我整整一周都在犹他州。我回到家，他正在处理一切。 (00:57:43)：如果你的家庭生活平衡，你的事业将会更加成功。就像阴和阳一样。如果有什么东西失去平衡，它就会吞没另一边。无论是你的工作还是你的家庭生活。尤其是，我们有三个孩子。由于我们俩的职业要求很高，真正平衡这一点非常困难。这并不是逆向思维，而是我们在做出决定时根本没有考虑到的事情。我们认为和这个人在一起有趣吗？这个人是我们认为与之在一起的人吗？但我的问题是这段关系对你的职业生涯有什么影响？ (00:58:14)：这个人是在举起你还是在推你？这个人会成为你最好的啦啦队长，还是会成为你最大的负担？您认为 20 年、30 年后这将如何体现？我认为这只是我希望我们更多地考虑的事情，我特别鼓励年轻人考虑这一点。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Such a great point. What I want now is a guide for vetting these things when you're dating. Deb's guide to dating.
turns.zh: 这是一个很好的观点。我现在想要的是约会时审查这些事情的指南。黛布的约会指南。

turns.speaker: Deb Liu
turns.en: I need to write that. Although I've only really dated him, the one person, so maybe I am like the worst person to tell.
turns.zh: 我需要写那个。虽然我只和他约会过，只有一个人，所以也许我是最难说出口的人。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: But it worked, so you're maybe the best person and now you look back.
turns.zh: 但这确实有效，所以你可能是最好的人，现在你回头看。

turns.speaker: Deb Liu
turns.en: That's right. That's right.
turns.zh: 这是正确的。这是正确的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And here's the questions I asked that worked. That's so funny. Okay, so before we get to our very exciting lightning round, is there anything else that you think might be helpful to share, something you might want to leave listeners with? Any other nuggets of wisdom or advice?
turns.zh: 这是我提出的有效问题。太有趣了。好的，在我们开始激动人心的闪电回合之前，您认为还有什么可以分享的，或者您可能想留给听众的东西吗？还有其他智慧或建议吗？

turns.speaker: Deb Liu
turns.en: Well, there's one quote which I share, I thought about when you were speaking earlier, which is about people who are resilient, which is life... This is a quote from Chuck Swindoll, he's a Christian writer I used to read a lot and it was, "Life is 10% what happens to you and 90% how you react to it." And I just looked him up recently and he actually published a book with that quote. He actually had that quote in a previous book from 20 years ago. (00:59:34): And I just think that's so important. You don't get to choose everything that happens in your life. So much is just, it just happens, but it's the people who choose a way forward to turn stumbling blocks and the stepping stones. As I said, "Somebody who actually says, 'you know what? I didn't get the job that I wanted and I'm just going to figure out another path,' those are the people who have the most successful and satisfying careers." They're thinking when other people are zagging vice versa. And I think that there are the ones who are the most resilient and happy in the long term.
turns.zh: 嗯，我分享了一句名言，当你早些时候发言时，我想到了这句话，它是关于有韧性的人，这就是生活……这是查克·斯温多尔（Chuck Swindoll）的一句话，他是一位基督教作家，我以前读过很多，它是，“生活有 10% 是发生在你身上的事情，90% 是你对它的反应。”我最近查了一下他，他实际上出版了一本引用这句话的书。事实上，他在 20 年前的一本书中引用过这句话。 (00:59:34)：我认为这非常重要。你无法选择生活中发生的一切。一切都是正义的，它只是发生了，但正是人们选择了一条前进的道路，以扭转绊脚石和踏脚石。正如我所说，“有人实际上会说，‘你知道吗？我没有得到我想要的工作，我只是想找到另一条路’，这些人是拥有最成功、最令人满意的职业生涯的人。”当其他人在拐弯抹角时，他们却在思考，反之亦然。我认为从长远来看，有些人是最有弹性和最快乐的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's such a good circle back to one of your first pieces of advice of just most successful people are people that are resilient and don't avoid failure, but embrace it and find a way to turn that around. I think it's such an important point. It's so hard to do. I guess just, I don't know, just to follow this thread a little bit, is there anything that has helped you build that? Has that always been the way your mind worked? I imagine coaching helps this, helps people with this." Is there anything just like that?
turns.zh: 这是一个很好的循环，回到你的第一条建议，大多数成功人士都是有韧性的人，不会避免失败，而是拥抱失败并找到扭转局面的方法。我认为这是非常重要的一点。这太难做到了。我想只是，我不知道，只是稍微跟随这个线程，有什么可以帮助你构建它吗？你的思维一直都是这样运作的吗？我想教练可以帮助人们做到这一点。”有类似的事情吗？

turns.speaker: Deb Liu
turns.en: Coaching is incredible for that. We joke it's work therapy, but really I think it's... For a long time I saw failure as this catastrophic thing. I was one of those kids who's like, "You never got a B until..." Then I got to college and I was like, "Wow, this is harder than I thought." And so I got two B's in college and I'm like, "I'm never doing that again." But I was that kid who always got the A, who got the great scores. I just thought that my life would end if I got a B which by the way is super unhealthy. (01:01:00): And looking back, I realized that work is not like that at all. And every time I got bad feedback I'm like, "This is catastrophic." But if you look at feedback as an opportunity, then it's very different. It's like this is a gift. I would be crushed. Every time I get a review no matter what rating I got, I would read the things that people would say and I was like, "Oh my gosh, I'm a terrible person." And I had to really rethink that. And I think coaching, leadership coaching has really helped me through that to say, "No, how do you process this and how do you get to the other side?" (01:01:33): And that has been so transformative for me is to have that outlet to actually talk through. No, no, no. What they're saying is not that you're a bad product person, it's that you need to do a better job communicating or connecting. And I really struggled with that. I was very transactional. I was not a connector. I was not warm. I really struggled with relationships. And a lot of the feedback I received for many years is this relationship issue. And it took me a long time to realize that people aren't saying this because I'm a bad person or that they hate me, but because they want to connect. (01:02:03): I was actually making it hard. And I think sometimes we take things so personally that it becomes kind of this thing. It is your white whale. It's like the thing you're chasing, but then what if you say, "You know what, I don't need to do that. I don't need to chase that. Instead I need to figure out what's behind the feedback and what are they trying to say?" And then actually change yourself over a long period of time towards that.
turns.zh: 对此，教练是不可思议的。我们开玩笑说这是工作疗法，但实际上我认为这是……很长一段时间以来，我将失败视为灾难性的事情。我是那些喜欢“你从来没有得到B直到......”的孩子之一，然后我上了大学，我想，“哇，这比我想象的要难。”所以我在大学得到了两个 B，我想，“我再也不会这样做了。”但我是那个总是得A的孩子，成绩很好。我只是想，如果我得了 B，我的生命就会结束，顺便说一句，这是超级不健康的。 (01:01:00)：回想起来，我意识到工作根本不是那样的。每次我收到不好的反馈时，我都会想，“这是灾难性的。”但如果你将反馈视为一个机会，那就大不一样了。就好像这是一份礼物。我会被压垮的。每次我收到评论时，无论我得到什么评级，我都会阅读人们会说的话，然后我就会想，“天哪，我是一个糟糕的人。”我必须重新思考这一点。我认为教练、领导力教练确实帮助我解决了这个问题，“不，你如何处理这个问题以及如何到达另一边？” (01:01:33)：对我来说，改变是因为有一个可以真正交谈的渠道。不，不，不。他们所说的并不是你是一个糟糕的产品人员，而是你需要更好地进行沟通或联系。我真的很挣扎。我非常善于交易。我不是一个连接器。我不热。我真的很挣扎于人际关系。多年来我收到的很多反馈都是这个关系问题。我花了很长时间才意识到人们这么说并不是因为我是一个坏人或者他们讨厌我，而是因为他们想要联系。 (01:02:03)：我实际上让事情变得困难了。我认为有时我们把事情看得太个人化，以至于事情变成了这样。这是你的白鲸。这就像你正在追逐的东西，但如果你说：“你知道吗，我不需要那样做。我不需要追逐那个。相反，我需要弄清楚反馈背后的内容以及他们想说什么？”然后在很长一段时间内真正改变自己以实现这一目标。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I had similar challenges where I had this pretty real imposter syndrome for a while when I started doing well. And a coach was the key for me to help me get over that and see that if I made a mistake. Things wouldn't crumble. And that it's very normal to make mistakes. Nobody will-
turns.zh: 我也遇到过类似的挑战，当我开始表现良好时，我有一段时间患有这种真正的冒名顶替综合症。教练是我的关键，可以帮助我克服这个问题，并看到我是否犯了错误。事情不会崩溃。犯错误是很正常的。没有人会——

turns.speaker: Deb Liu
turns.en: And by the way, I think perfectionism is a curse we place on ourselves. And it's a very dangerous thing, particularly for product leaders because product managers, you know things are going to go wrong. That's literally part of your job. And yet when we have perfectionism, it is a lack of trust in our ability to bounce back and our ability to actually adapt. But the more adaptable you are, the less you have to be perfect every single time.
turns.zh: 顺便说一句，我认为完美主义是我们对自己的诅咒。这是一件非常危险的事情，特别是对于产品负责人来说，因为产品经理，你知道事情会出错。这实际上是你工作的一部分。然而，当我们有完美主义时，我们就缺乏对自己恢复能力和实际适应能力的信任。但你的适应能力越强，你就越不需要每次都做到完美。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Just to leave people with a tactical piece of advice, say they are like, "Oh man, I need a coach," do you have any advice for how to find a coach? How to explore that route?
turns.zh: 只是为了给人们提供战术建议，让他们说，“哦，伙计，我需要一名教练”，你对如何寻找教练有什么建议吗？如何探索该路线？

turns.speaker: Deb Liu
turns.en: So I actually wrote an article, because one of the things I struggle with coaching is very expensive often, and not every company provides it. My husband actually works at a coaching company called Sounding Board to make it more accessible. But one of the things I encourage people to do is there are other ways to get coaches. I'm in a lean-in group and we are just like, we support each other. I'm in a coaching circle in YPO, so that's a group of CEOs. And I'm in a number of these coaching circles, which give you an opportunity to learn from each other and to get pure coaching. And I think that's a great place to start, especially early in your career when you're seeing the same people making the same mistakes. (01:03:54): I think as you get more senior, having an individual coach helps because the situations are so much more unique. But I do think that having that outlet, having a place to say, "Hey, is it me or is this situation not right? And how should I think through this?" That's so incredibly important.
turns.zh: 所以我实际上写了一篇文章，因为我在辅导中遇到的困难之一通常是非常昂贵的，而且并不是每个公司都提供它。我丈夫实际上在一家名为 Sounding Board 的教练公司工作，以使其更容易接近。但我鼓励人们做的一件事是通过其他方式获得教练。我在一个精益小组中，我们就像，我们互相支持。我在 YPO 的教练圈子里，所以这是一群首席执行官。我在很多这样的教练圈子里，这让你有机会互相学习并获得纯粹的教练。我认为这是一个很好的起点，尤其是在你职业生涯的早期，当你看到同样的人犯同样的错误时。 (01:03:54)：我认为当你的资历越来越高时，拥有一名单独的教练会有所帮助，因为情况更加独特。但我确实认为，有了这个出口，就有一个地方可以说：“嘿，是我的问题还是这种情况不对？我应该如何思考这个问题？”这非常重要。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I'm listening to this book, or reading a book called Listen right now that a previous guest recommended. It's a parenting book and it's about just the power of listening and how much that solves many problems with your challenges or with your child. When your child is having a problem just listening to them. There's a lot of power. This came from a coach that was on the podcast recently. [inaudible 01:04:31]
turns.zh: 我正在听这本书，或者正在阅读前一位客人推荐的一本名为《Listen now》的书。这是一本育儿书，讲述的是倾听的力量，以及倾听可以在多大程度上解决你面临的挑战或孩子的许多问题。当您的孩子遇到问题时，只需倾听他们的意见即可。有很大的力量。这是最近在播客上的一位教练说的。 [听不清 01:04:31]

turns.speaker: Deb Liu
turns.en: Sounds great. I'll definitely, I'll read it or listen to it.
turns.zh: 听起来很棒。我一定会，我会读它或听它。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I know it's weird. I'm like reading, it's called Listen. He's like, "This is the only parenting book you need really. It solves all the problems that we deal with." So anyway, that was an awesome final nugget that I'm glad we got there. With that though, we've reached our very exciting lightning round. Are you ready?
turns.zh: 我知道这很奇怪。我喜欢读书，这叫听。他说，“这是你真正需要的唯一一本育儿书。它解决了我们处理的所有问题。”所以无论如何，这是一个很棒的最后的金块，我很高兴我们到达了那里。尽管如此，我们已经进入了非常激动人心的闪电回合。你准备好了吗？

turns.speaker: Deb Liu
turns.en: Let's do it.
turns.zh: 我们开始做吧。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Let's do it. First question, what are two or three books that you've most recommended to other people?
turns.zh: 我们开始做吧。第一个问题，您最常向其他人推荐的两三本书是什么？

turns.speaker: Deb Liu
turns.en: So I love the book from Professor Jeffrey Pfeffer. I speak in his class now that I read it way before that, it's called Power: Who Has It and Why. I love the book. He actually has the more practical one, 7 Rules of Power, which came out more recently. And so it's a book that reminds us that power is not accidental, that people often get it for different reasons and how you should think about the playing field. (01:05:23): Another book is The Conversation, Dr. Livingston wrote that about race in America, and I just love that it's a very honest assessment of race in America. It's hard to have that conversation and I love that he uses a lot of facts and encourages people to open up and have conversations around it. And then the last one I would say is, well, Susan Cain's Quiet. I adore the book because I do have introverted kids. I myself am introverted and just to read the power of introverts as a reminder that we do have amazing people who don't communicate the same way. (01:05:59): I love that it's a tribute to the success of those. Even if our workplace is not adapted to it, I do think we need to adapt to it so that we can bring the best in everybody. But her book is a reminder that there's so much power even in silence.
turns.zh: 所以我喜欢杰弗里·普费弗教授的这本书。我在他的课上发言，因为我在那之前就读过这本书，它的名字叫《权力：谁拥有它以及为什么》。我喜欢这本书。他实际上有更实用的一个，即最近发布的《权力的七条规则》。因此，这本书提醒我们，权力不是偶然的，人们经常因为不同的原因而获得权力，以及你应该如何思考竞争环境。 (01:05:23)：另一本书是《对话》，利文斯顿博士写了关于美国种族的书，我很喜欢它对美国种族的非常诚实的评估。进行这样的对话很困难，我喜欢他使用大量事实并鼓励人们敞开心扉并围绕它进行对话。我要说的最后一个是苏珊·凯恩的《安静》。我喜欢这本书，因为我确实有内向的孩子。我本人很内向，只是想通过阅读内向者的力量来提醒我们，我们确实有一些很棒的人，他们的沟通方式不同。 (01:05:59)：我喜欢这是对这些人的成功的致敬。即使我们的工作场所不适应它，我确实认为我们需要适应它，这样我们才能让每个人都发挥出最好的一面。但她的书提醒我们，即使在沉默中也有如此大的力量。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: The first book you mentioned Jeffrey Pfeffer, he's been on the podcast. I think he may have mentioned you in our conversation or-
turns.zh: 你提到的第一本书杰弗里·普费弗（Jeffrey Pfeffer），他一直在播客上。我想他可能在我们的谈话中提到了你或者-

turns.speaker: Deb Liu
turns.en: I love Professor Pfeffer.
turns.zh: 我爱普费弗教授。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That was a fun conversation because I came into it very nervous for what his advice would be and then came up with it being like, "This is great. This is-"
turns.zh: 那是一次有趣的谈话，因为我对他的建议感到非常紧张，然后想到的是，“这太棒了。这是——”

turns.speaker: Deb Liu
turns.en: He is very wise,
turns.zh: 他非常聪明，

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: He's very wise and just very, "I don't care what you think, I'm just going to tell you the reality of the world." Oh man. Okay. Next question. Do you have a favorite recent movie or TV show that you've really enjoyed?
turns.zh: 他非常聪明，而且非常“我不在乎你怎么想，我只是要告诉你世界的现实。”噢，伙计。好的。下一个问题。您最近有最喜欢的电影或电视节目吗？

turns.speaker: Deb Liu
turns.en: Okay. I know this is a fandom thing, but I love Fallout. So I played the game Fallout 4 last year, and then the show came out and it was amazing. And I know that sounds so nerdy, but it was incredible. And I know that video game movie annotations tend to be terrible, but it was so great and having played the game it was even better. Is that super nerdy?
turns.zh: 好的。我知道这是粉丝的事情，但我喜欢《辐射》。所以我去年玩了《辐射 4》这个游戏，然后这个节目出来了，真是太棒了。我知道这听起来很书呆子气，但这真是令人难以置信。我知道视频游戏电影注释往往很糟糕，但它太棒了，玩过游戏后感觉更好。这是超级书呆子吗？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: No, I watched Fallout. I don't know anything about the game, but the show itself was really fun. Just I had no idea what I was even getting into. So no. Acceptable nerdy level. I don't know if you can get too nerdy on this show. Next question, do you have a favorite product you recently discovered that you just really like?
turns.zh: 不，我看过《辐射》。我对这个游戏一无所知，但节目本身真的很有趣。只是我根本不知道自己在做什么。所以不。可以接受的书呆子水平。我不知道你在这个节目中是否会变得太书呆子。下一个问题是，您最近发现了您真正喜欢的最喜欢的产品吗？

turns.speaker: Deb Liu
turns.en: Well, so actually what's really interesting is I never got into Twitter. I just couldn't figure it out. Recently I really got into Threads and I didn't think I would. I was like, "Well, just post some stuff on it," but really I just love... I could never figure out Twitter. You follow the wrong person and the whole thing, it's terrible. If somebody is posting too much or too little, but there's something about the Threads algorithm that's really worked. The first few months wasn't quite there, but I just feel like it's spot on and now I see the magic of it.
turns.zh: 嗯，实际上真正有趣的是我从来没有上过 Twitter。我就是想不通。最近我真正迷上了Threads，但我认为我不会。我当时想，“好吧，就在上面发布一些东西吧”，但我真的很喜欢……我永远无法弄清楚 Twitter。你追随了错误的人以及整个事情，这太可怕了。如果有人发帖太多或太少，但线程算法确实有效。最初的几个月并不完全如此，但我只是觉得它恰到好处，现在我看到了它的魔力。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's so interesting. I've seen some stats that it's bigger than X now slash Twitter and I wonder if that's true. I got to look that up, but I've seen more activity on Threads. So maybe I need to go back there. I spent some time around-
turns.zh: 那太有趣了。我看到一些统计数据显示它比 X 现在削减 Twitter 还要大，我想知道这是否属实。我必须查一下，但我在线程上看到了更多活动。所以也许我需要回到那里。我花了一些时间-

turns.speaker: Deb Liu
turns.en: Cheering from the sidelines that it's successful because I use it a lot now. And I guess I had never had a place for realtime news and it's not exactly meant to be newsy, but maybe it's just who I follow, but I love just seeing like, "Here's five headlines you probably missed." And I was like, "Oh." I know they're trying to downplay politics, but I just love that it feels like you get a glimpse of what's going on in the world in five minutes."
turns.zh: 在场外欢呼它是成功的，因为我现在经常使用它。我想我从来没有一个地方可以看到实时新闻，而且它并不完全意味着新闻，但也许这只是我关注的人，但我喜欢看到这样的内容，“这是你可能错过的五个头条新闻。”我当时想，“哦。”我知道他们试图淡化政治，但我就是喜欢这种感觉，就像你在五分钟内就能一睹世界上正在发生的事情。”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. Two more questions. Do you have a favorite life motto that you often think about, come back to, share with friends or family find useful in work or in life?
turns.zh: 好的。还有两个问题。您是否有一条最喜欢的人生格言，您经常思考、回想并与朋友或家人分享，并发现它在工作或生活中有用？

turns.speaker: Deb Liu
turns.en: Ooh, that's a good question. Well, actually, I would say that it's very similar to the Chuck Swindoll one about life. So we can use that.
turns.zh: 哦，这是个好问题。嗯，实际上，我想说这与查克·斯温多尔的人生观非常相似。所以我们可以使用它。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Great. That's what I imagined because you shared that one early on. And I imagine that was going to be your answer. Final question, you started Facebook Marketplace, you built it. Now, it has a billion users, more than that. What's the most interesting thing that you have bought or sold on Facebook Marketplace?
turns.zh: 伟大的。这就是我的想象，因为你很早就分享了这一点。我想这就是你的答案。最后一个问题，您创建了 Facebook Marketplace，并构建了它。现在，它拥有十亿用户，甚至更多。您在 Facebook Marketplace 上购买或出售的最有趣的东西是什么？

turns.speaker: Deb Liu
turns.en: The best thing I ever sold on there was I sold my minivan on it and in four days. I made my husband do it because I wanted him to test the product. We were selling our minivan and I'm like, "Just try Facebook Marketplace." He's like, "I don't know about this." And he's like, "There's too many people contacting me. I needed it to stop." So it worked really well for us. I think I have bought so many things on there. It's actually sort of embarrassing. (01:09:30): Recently, my daughter wanted the same desk as I had for her new room and they no longer sell it at Costco. And I found it for half the price from a woman who was moving and she's like, "Here," and I love it. So I bought probably way too many things on Facebook Marketplace actually. But it's a great thing. I actually use it as a great rental for kid stuff because you buy a kid's bike and then when they outgrow it, you sell it back. (01:09:56): And the rental fee is almost free and I don't have the store all of it. So I love every part of it. I still am an admin user and I send a lot of feedback back to that team still.
turns.zh: 我在那里卖过的最好的东西是我在四天内卖掉了我的小型货车。我让我丈夫这样做是因为我想让他测试该产品。我们正在出售我们的小型货车，我想，“试试 Facebook Marketplace。”他说：“我不知道这件事。”他说，“有太多人联系我。我需要停止。”所以它对我们来说非常有效。我想我在那里买了很多东西。其实这有点尴尬。 (01:09:30)：最近，我女儿想要在她的新房间使用与我相同的桌子，但 Costco 不再出售它。我以一半的价格从一位正在搬家的女士那里找到了它，她说，“在这里，”我喜欢它。所以我实际上在 Facebook Marketplace 上买了太多东西。但这是一件很棒的事情。事实上，我用它来出租儿童用品，因为你买了一辆儿童自行车，当他们长大了，用不完时，你就把它卖回来。 (01:09:56)：而且租金几乎是免费的，而且我没有商店的全部。所以我喜欢它的每一部分。我仍然是管理员用户，并且仍然向该团队发送大量反馈。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's amazing. Deb, this was amazing. I'm so happy we made time for this. Thank you so much for coming on. Two final questions. Where can folks find you if they want to reach out, maybe read about stuff you're doing? Where's your Substack and anything else people can check out?
turns.zh: 太棒了。黛布，这太棒了。我很高兴我们为此腾出了时间。非常感谢您的光临。最后两个问题。如果人们想要联系你，或者阅读你正在做的事情，他们可以在哪里找到你？您的子堆栈以及人们可以查看的其他内容在哪里？

turns.speaker: Deb Liu
turns.en: Yeah, so debliu.substack if you want to look. I post probably about once a week. I'm on LinkedIn, I'm on Threads, so please do find me.
turns.zh: 是的，如果你想看的话，那么 debliu.substack 。我大概每周发一次帖子。我在 LinkedIn、Threads 上，所以请找到我。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And then the actual final question, how can listeners be useful to you?
turns.zh: 然后是真正的最后一个问题，听众如何对你有用？

turns.speaker: Deb Liu
turns.en: Well, I would just love to hear what you heard from today that resonated with you and what you're going to do with it.
turns.zh: 好吧，我很想听听您今天听到的与您产生共鸣的内容以及您将如何处理。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And how would they share that LinkedIn or at Threads?
turns.zh: 他们将如何在 LinkedIn 或 Threads 上分享该信息？

turns.speaker: Deb Liu
turns.en: I'm happy to read your comments or send it if you want to-
turns.zh: 我很高兴阅读您的评论或如果您愿意的话将其发送-

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: There we go.
turns.zh: 我们开始吧。

turns.speaker: Deb Liu
turns.en: ... send it to me. If you've actually subscribed to my Substack, you can just reply to the first email and then I get it.
turns.zh: ...发送给我。如果您确实订阅了我的 Substack，您只需回复第一封电子邮件，然后我就会收到它。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. But the easy way, as you said, are replying to YouTube comments. There we go. Get people to YouTube, click that subscribe button. Deb, thank you so much for being here and thank you.
turns.zh: 惊人的。但正如您所说，最简单的方法是回复 YouTube 评论。我们开始吧。让人们访问 YouTube，点击订阅按钮。黛布，非常感谢你来到这里，谢谢你。

turns.speaker: Deb Liu
turns.en: Thank you so much, Lenny. It's great.
turns.zh: 非常感谢你，莱尼。这很棒。

turns.zh: 再见，大家。非常感谢您的聆听。如果您发现这很有价值，您可以在 Apple Podcasts、Spotify 或您最喜欢的播客应用程序上订阅该节目。另外，请考虑给我们评分或留下评论，因为这确实有助于其他听众找到播客。您可以在 lennyspodcast.com 上找到所有过去的剧集或了解有关该节目的更多信息。下一集见。
